Then I add-and I think this is the strongest argument-that so long as we have but punitive laws it will be impossible to stop that evil. You cannot have a punitive law applied to a particular evil unless public opinion admits that that particular evil is a crime. The public at large are not interested in this, and a great number who are interested are something like the gamblers in other things : some of them are not disposed to have the law changed, and others say that evil exists in every country and it is useless to try and stop it_ in this. It is also argued that it will be impossible to convince a great many people, and even the judges themselves, that speculation in itself is a crime and that therefore it is useless to apply a punitive law.
What we need is an administrative law ; a law that will not prevent legitimate speculation, but a law that will minimize speculation ; a law that will regulate speculation and that will establish a basis of some kind for stock exchange operations, and in consequence prevent wild speculation. First of all, I believe that stock brokers should conduct their business under the authority of the law, just as hotel keepers do, and just as in large cities people who keep houses that are not considered to the credit of the community, but are necessary to a state of corruption, must keep these houses under the guidance of the law. Stock brokers should take out a license. I do not say that they should be appointed by the government, because that was tried in France and proved to be a failure. But stock brokers should take out a license so that we may know who is conducting stock exchange operations, and so that nobody else shall be authorized to carry on the same trade.
Then it should be made a provision of the law that no large company, whether incorporated by parliament or under the seal of the Secretary of State, can elect as a director a licensed stock broker. Then again, stock brokers should have no right to speculate for themselves, but should content themselves with the profit arising from the speculation of their clients. If speculation is made by them under a false name it should be assimilated to conspiracy.
Then the question of margin comes in. I must say that I share the opinion which was expressed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce fifteen years ago, that so long as we allow speculation on narrow margins, it
will be very difficult to stop the evil. I believe it would be impossible at the present time to declare that no transfer of shares could be made unless they should be paid for in full, and it might not be wise to enact that now ; but it should be at least declared that no transfer of shares can be made unless they are margined to the extent of at least 25 per cent of their value. This system of purchasing on small margins is the greatest cause of slumps. Shares of good and bad stocks are bought in large quantity by people who put all the money they have on a small margin, and who, therefore, take the greater risk, because they expect the greater profit. They buy on these small margins just for the purpose of selling as soon as the shares rise in value : and this gives the greatest opportunity to the ' bears,' because when they want to run down a stock they know that thousands of shares of that stock are in the hands of people who cannot hold them and who are bound to sell the moment they go down a few points. When the bears make a raid, and the stock goes down three or four points, these people are forced to sell, and then the slump begins. The next day those who are a little stronger on the market will be forced to sell, and within a week or ten days the different grades of these small speculators will be wiped out ; and such wild be the decrease in the value of shares caused by putting so many on the market, that the bona fide holders of the stock, who invested with the idea of becoming part owners in that property, will also be wiped out of their holdings. Therefore, the larger the margin you provide for, the safer you will make the speculation. If the stock is fully paid up, or if it is paid up to a large extent, the stockholders will look to the directors for a profitable administration of the concern. They will look to the directors of the company for their security, instead of looking to Mr. Forget or to Mr. Ames to make them gain upon stocks that perhaps Mr. Forget or Mr. Ames are interested in running down.
In the fourth place, I would advise the Minister of Justice and the government to give some attention to the existing law concerning joint stock companies. I am told, although I hope it is not the case, that at present the Secretary of State issues under the Great Seal of Canada letters-patent authorizing the directors of companies of various kinds to issue paid-up stock to almost an unlimited amount. I need not say what a cursed operation this issue of paid-up stock is. We all know what was the result in the case of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company. This company had already obligations for more than its property was worth, and just because it pleased its directors, they made a new issue of $5,000,000 worth of common stock at 60 per cent. It was not because it was worth 60 per cent, but just because they decided, under

tlieir authority, that it was to be sold at 60 per cent. And when two of the kings of the financial world, Mr. Ross and Mr. Forget, decided to quarrel and to make the shareholders pay for their quarrel, the stock was run down to 12 or 13 per cent. I therefore say that there should be no authorization given to any company authorized by this parliament or by the Secretary of State, to issue stock or obligations for anything else than real worth, which would in itself justify such issue of stock or obligations.
I would also advise that the law should provide that no transfer of shares would be valid unless the transfer bore the name of the seller and the purchaser and the date of the transfer, so that we would not have these pretended sales that are now carried on, and so that when the speculator on margin would come to pay in full for his shares he would receive the shares that he bought and not the shares that the stock broker bought when it pleased him or paid him to do so.
Then the law should provide that at least the savings banks, if not all the banks ; at least the savings banks that are authorized by this parliament under the credit of the country and which receive the money of the workingmen and the poorer classes, should be debarred from being a party to these speculations, and while they refuse to accept a good note signed by an honest and solvent man, endorsed by another honest man, for say $500, they will not be permitted to lend $50,000 to Mr. Ames or Mr. Forget, who will give them as security shares that are not their own property, but which belong to other people, and with which they play football all the year round. At all events, no bank, whether a chartered bank or a savings bank, should be authorized to lend money on stocks that are not margined to at least 25 per cent of their value.
It may be said that these suggestions would to a large extent stop the operations of the stock exchanges. I am not a high financier and I cannot say what the result would be if stock exchange operations were limited, but I share in the opinion of the member for North Norfolk (Mr. Charlton) when he said, that these operations could be greatly curtailed without any detriment whatever to the community. I have always thought that the idea that people should be left to speculate as widely as they want is a wrong idea, kept up by stock brokers for their own purposes. Even the pe pie who have been fleeced by them are accomplices of such a false opinion. At any rate no damage will be done to legitimate speculation if the hand of the law separates the good from the bad, the robbers from the robbed, and protects those who are fleeced from those who fleece them. I have spoken at great length and it may be that the newspapers will say of me, as they said a month ago, that I speak feelingly because I have been injured by these people. I wish Mr. BOURASSA.
to say, not because it is of any importance, that I have never in my life had any dealings with stock brokers, that I have never speculated, that I do not even know what it is to speculate, except by the sad relations which I have received from people who are just as intelligent, just as honest, just as good business men as those who have robbed them under the protection of the law.
What is the Act ?
The Central Canada Loan & Savings Company, Chap. 97. I do not say on" single word against this company, for I believe it is an exceedingly prosperous and well-managed company.
Then the Act is all right ?

No, that company has the power, and it depends entirely upon its management whether it will exercise that power or not. Let me read the powers that are given it:
The new company shall have the power to lend moneys on the security of, or purchase or invest in-
(a.) mortgages or hypothecs upon freehold or leasehold real estate, or other immovables ;
(b.) the debentures, bonds, stocks and other securties of any government or any municipal
corporation or school corporation, or any chartered bank

The only thing I was able to accomplish- and I only succeeded in doing it after a great deal of pressure and after showing the evils that would result if my suggestion were not adopted-was to have these words put in :
-to the extent of not more than twenty per cent of the paid up capital stock of any such bank

That clause has been added to the charter of every other company of a similar nature since then.
-or incorporated company, if incorporated by or under the authority of the parliament of Canada, or of the legislature of any former or present or any future province of Canada; provided that the new company shall not lend upon the security of, or purchase or invest in bills of exchange or promissory notes.
The new company may borrow money and receive money upon deposit, upon such terms as to interest, security and otherwise as may be agreed on, and may issue its bonds, debentures and other securities for moneys borrowed; provided always that the total of the new company's liabilities to the public outstanding from time to time shall not exceed four times the amount paid upon its capital stock; and provided further that the amount held on deposit shall not at any time exceed the aggregate amount of its then paid-up and unimpaired capital and of its cash actually in hand or deposited in any chartered bank in Canada and belonging to the new company.
So long as the new company is indebted for money received upon deposit, the total amount of its real estate and its mortgages or hypothecs upon freehold or leasehold real estate or immovables shall not, from time to time exceed eighty per cent of its total assets
The new company shall transmit, on or before the 1st of March in each year, to the Minister of Finance and Receiver General, a statement in duplicate, to the 31st December, inclusive, of the previous year, verified by the oath of the president or vice-president and the manager, setting out the capital stock of the new company and the proportion thereof paid-up, the assets and liabilities of the new company, the amount and nature of the investments made by the new company, both on its own behalf and on the behalf of others, and the average rate of interest derived therefrom, distinguishing the classes of securities, and also the extent and value of the lands held by it, and such other details as to the nature and extent of the business of the new company as the Minister of Finance and the Receiver General requires, and in such form and with such details as he from time to time requires and prescribes ; but the new company shall in no case be bound to disclose the name or private affairs of any person who has dealings with it.
That charter, against the protest of the banks of Canada, was passed by this House, although the evils to which it would give rise were pointed out very strongly by myself and one or two others. I am within the mark when I say that at least fifteen. or twenty other companies have come to this House and obtained the same powers. It was under a similar clause that the two

unfortunate companies in St. Tliomas came to grief. They made foolish investments, under the authority of this clause, which they could not have made had that power not been given them. They had the right under their charters to invest their whole capital and deposits in the wildest of wild cat mining schemes. They could, between the 1st of January and any time one or two months after, invest all their capital, and it would be fifteen months after that date before the shareholders would learn how their money had been invested. You cannot by any law prevent people speculating in some thing or other. People who will not smoke, people who will not indulge In cigarettes or drink, will bet on borse races, and the sooner we will recognize this universal tendency of our human nature, the better. But there is one way in which a government can minimize the evil, and that is by taking great care that all companies, having the stamp and authority of government, shall be subject to restrictions in this respect and be forced-especially all companies which borrow money and invest it in such fluctuating securities-to send out to the shareholders and the public, at short dates, statements showing the condition of their affairs, just as the banks have to do. Just imagine what the condition would be if our banks were not required from month to month to give their statements to the public. That is a check which keeps banking within its proper limits and prevents abuse. How can you prevent men in a town like St. Thomas from buying on margin, when they are told that the directors of this, that and the other company are piling up profits by speculation ? That is what was the trouble in St. Thomas. Those directors gave out that they were making large sums of money out of stocks, and I dare say they did for a time, and the result was a perfect craze of wild speculation in that district, from which it has suffered very seriously, apart altogether from these particular failures. This government has laid itself open to blame by giving a free hand to financial companies applying for incorporation.

Had either the companies referred to authority in its Act of incorporation to buy stocks on margin ?
Mr. OSLER, They could do anything they liked.
I would like the hon. gentleman to read the clause which gave them authority to buy stocks on margin.

One need not buy stocks on margin to lose money. As a matter of fact, these companies have the power to buy stocks on margin, because they can lend money to any individual to enable that individual to buy stocks. They also bought Mr. OSLER.
stocks on margin themselves. That is shown by the reports we have so far.

Whether or not the powers given to these loan companies were too great or too little is a fair subject of debate, and I am not going to assert that our legislation is in all respects perfect. But I am rather surprised to learn from the hon. gentleman of the heroic efforts which he made to prevent the government giving certain powers to these companies. 1 have no recollection of any such efforts or of the measure to which he refers, but, according to his own statement, it was a private Bill. Of course, the government, in a sense, are responsible for all legislation, and in that respect we have to accept responsibility ; but the responsibility is not limited to the government, but is shared by every hon. member who votes for the measure. My recollection of the matter in question is that it was in no sense a party measure ; and in looking through 'Hansard' hurriedly, I cannot find that my hon. friend ever opened his mouth against it. It may be that in the Banking and Commerce Committee my hon. friend gave expression to his valuable views ; but I should imagine, if lie had very strong views and thought it a matter so important, he would not have been content to confine his observations to that committee, but would have come before the House and put himself on record against the clause. From the hurried glance I have been able to give over * Hansard,' I cannot find that there was any debate on the Bill. In the index there is no reference, under the name of my hon. friend, to this Bill. If in the Banking and Commerce Committee he expressed the views he has just now given to the House and others differed from him, of course, he is entitled to credit to that extent. But. if he implies that this was a great question as between the government and the opposition, or that on this question the government insisted upon the adoption of a certain course by this legislature against his judgment and that of hon. gentlemen opposite, that is hardly a fair presentation of the case. Many a clause appears in private Bills which is the subject of discussion, and it would hardly be justifiable for an hon. gentleman, years afterwards, to say that they were all the work of the government. The hon. gentleman will have to share with us some of this responsibility, when it does not appear that he made any effort to prevent the passing of the clause, even to the extent of voting agains it.
speakername: The MINISTER OP FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

speechtext:
The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Fielding) is right. I do not remember having taken any steps against it in this House. I knew it was useless. A protest, a very strong protest, was made in the committee. But the Finance Minister appeared and championed the Bill a's strong-

ly as I and some others opposed it, so I felt sure it was quite useless to go further in the matter. But to the extent of not raising my voice in protest in this House, I am responsible.

May I be permitted to contradict the hon. gentleman's statement (Mr. Osier's) on the personal point. He said that I appeared and championed the Bill. Nothing occurred that would justify that statement.

I would like to point out to the Finance Minister that I raised, in this House, during the present session, exactly the same objection as that spoken of by my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Osier) as having been raised by him years ago. This was in connection with Bill (No. 24), which is not a private, but a public Bill.
What Bill is that?

It is an Act to extend the power of loan companies.
I have it before me. The effect of the Bill was to confine its operation to a very few companies ; I think it was stated at the time that it was confined to practically one company. It did not contain exactly the provisions referred to with regard to the power to purchase shares in a bank. But I will read my hon. friend the Minister of Finance the clause, which I think, passed in exactly these words, with the exception I have mentioned :
1. Every loan company, in addition to the powers vested in it. may from time to time leud money on the security of, or purchase or invest in, (a.) mortgages or hypothecs upon freehold or leasehold real estate or other immovables, (b.) the debentures, bonds, stocks and other securities of any government or any municipal or school corporation, or of any chartered bank or incorporated company if incorporated by rhe parliament of Canada or by the legislature of any former or present or future province of Canada, but not including bills of exchange or promissory notes.
I raised the objection that this would enable this loan company-if it applied only to one company-to invest its moneys in the stock of any wild-cat company in Canada, and I did not think that was a judicious power to confer on any such company, as the results, in some case at least, woujd be very likely to be those pointed out by my hon. friend from West Toronto. The hon. Minister of Finance, if I remember correctly, said that the power had been granted to other loan companies, and no evil results had followed, and there did not appear to be any reason for withholding it from this company or the companies to which this Bill applied. I did protest against that policy. I thought it very bad policy to give these companies these enormous powers of investment and purchase. The Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) asked this question: Is a company of that kind authorized to purchase on margin? If that hon. gentleman had thought for a moment, be would have seen that that did not affect the question we are discussing. The hon. member for Labeile (Mr. Bourassa) also confused the matter very much in the remarks he made. But, suppose this company goes to a broker and says: We want to buy so much stock, and we will pay a margin of 10 or 20 per cent. Or, suppose it buys from the same broker that stock and then takes the stock to a bank and borrows against it all but 10 or 20 per cent. You may call one transaction gambling and the other transaction not gambling if you like. But, so far as the results are concerned, they must be the same upon the person who engages in the transaction.

The transaction is illegal on the part of the company. It may not be illegal on the part of the brokers, who may be incorporated with certain power as a stock exchange, but it would be illegal on the part of the loan company.
Illegal to purchase the stocks and then pledge them?
No, to buy them on margin.
I do not know how my hon. friend is going to make the distinction, so far as the results are concerned. The result to the unfortunate shareholders would be exactly the same.
I admit the result would be

Of course, the result would be the same. That emphasizes the point made by my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Osier). It is absolutely wrong to confer such wide powers on any loan company, the shareholders of which have the right to assume' that the funds placed in the bands of their directors shall be invested in securities which are not affected b'y the contingencies to which mining companies of various kinds are subject in this country.
My hon. friend from Labeile has taken up a good deal of time this afternoon. I do not propose to direct much attention to his remarks. The first and most important point is that, for the most part, his remarks seem to constitute an attack upon the private affairs of a gentleman in the city of Montreal who is not in this House to defend himself. So far as the speech of the hon. member for Labeile amounts to a personal attack, I am bound to say that I do not think it was in very good taste. I have heard very great indignation expressed in this House with regard to criticism of government officials, even in respect of a public matter, on the ground that they

were not here to defend themselves. But here, in respect not of a public matter, but of a private matter, we have the house of Messrs. Forget dragged before this parliament to the extent of an hour's speech, mainly devoted to the discussion of their private affairs. If these gentlemen are guilty of the dishonourable conduct the bon. member for Labelle has seen fit to attribute to them, the courts of the country are open to any who are aggrieved. For my part, I decline to believe any of the statements reflecting on these gentlemen. I decline also to believe that stock brokers, as a class, are the scoundrels that this bon. gentleman undertakes to say they are. I have no doubt that some stock brokers, as some members of any other class, are not honourable, may be even guilty of fraud. But, even though that is the case, it does not become any lion, gentleman in this House to stigmatize these men as gamblers, perpetrating fraud every day of their lives. When my hon. friend from Labelle talks about gambling he ought' to look at both sides of the case. If these brokers are gamblers, what are the men of whom he talks so sympathetically who give these brokers the instructions under which they act? If these stock brokers carry out the instructions that necessarily involve gambling, the men who give the instructions are as- much gamblers as tiie stock brokers themselves. My hon. friend (Mr. Bourassa) was very anxious, some time ago, for an investigation into these transactions. Perhaps he had better not go far away from this House to begin an investigation of that kind. And the investigation should not stop short at stock brokers. So far as the law is concerned, it has been put in operation in some parts of the country. I believe that in Nova Scotia indictments have been found against some stock brokers under the very section of the statutes to which my hon. friend has referred. But as to the remedies which are suggested by my hon. friend from Labelle, I should hardly think that he was very serious in some of those which he advanced to the House. One of the suggestions he made was, so far as I could understand him, that when any gentleman desired to take, as the term is 'a little flyer ' on stock, he should not be permitted to do so unless he put up a larger margin than is the custom at the present time; that is to say, he should be allowed to gamole, as the hon. member termed it, but he must gamble under certain precautions. I do not know whether that remedy would commend itself to the Minister of Justice, or whether he thinks that idea could be carried out. Now, I have no doubt that this dealing in stocks has become a great evil in Canada; but so have many other things become great evils. For example, as the hon. member for Toronto pointed out, we have had land booms in
Mr. BORDER (Halifax.-,
Oic North-west, we have had land booms in Manitoba, we have had land booms in the city of Winnipeg. I think even in the city of Toronto we have had something that was described ten or twelve years ago as a land boom.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) And Sydney, C.B.
The Toronto land boom was a reality.

Of course we all know that when people in any country see their friends making large sums of money by speculative means, by a sudden increment of value, whether in stocks, lauds or anything else, the community as a whole is very apt to' lose its head and to indulge in speculations that sooner or later will bring their logical and legitimate results. That is the condition of affairs in Canada at the present time. Prices of certain stocks in this country went up very suddenly and rapidly, people saw their friends around them making a great deal of money, and men who could not afford to take risks in anything, took risks in stocks. Some people went headlong into stock speculation and many of them most unfortunately lost everything they had. I doubt very much whether you can cure an evil of that kind by legislation. I am not prepared to say that you might not be able to mitigate it to some extent by legislation, in the way of amendments to the criminal code. No doubt, the Minister of Justice will turn his attention to that subject. But as for the remedies which the hon. member for Labelle has suggested, I do not see the slightest adequacy in any one of them. Suppose you licensed every broker in Canada and put him under periodical inspection from time to time, does not the hon. member for Labelle, who is so familiar with this subject, know that people all over Canada could speculate through brokers in the United States, as they do already ? The hon. member for Labelle. who is prepared to say that he knows that nine-tenths of the stock operations in Canada are in the nature of gambling, surely must be familiar with that fact, and I would like to know how he would deal with it. If you license every broker in Canada and put him under the most rigid inspection, you would still have people in Canada dealing with brokers in the United States.
Do we not license insurance companies ?

Well, we do license insurance companies, but I am bound to say that I do not exactly understand the relevancy of the hon. gentleman's question. If you licensed every broker in Canada, even if you abolished every broker in Canada, people in Canada would still have ample opportunity to speculate in stocks with United States brokers. So, I say, I

(Jo not believe that you can absolutely cure this evil by legislation, though, as I have already said, I am not prepared to say that the Minister of Justice might not mitigate it to some extent by" amendments to the criminal code, which would prevent these operations being conducted on so large a scale.
Now, the hon. member for Labelle took occasion also to reflect seriously upon their Lordships of the Privy Council. I have no doubt they will be very much pained when they learn that their decision does not commend itself to his own sound and well considered judgment. I think the hon. member for Labelle perhaps overlooked the fact, when he was contrasting the Law Lords with the members of the Judicial Committee, that those two bodies are composed of exactly the same learned judges. At least that was the case up to a few years ago, I have not examined the personnel of those two bodies lately. But I know that a few years ago every Law Lord was a member of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, and I think that is the case still with the possible exception of the Chief Justice. When the hon. member reflects in scathing language upon the legal acumen of the members of the Judicial Committee, he reflects on the legal acumen of the Law Lords who are exactly the same persons.
Mr. BOtfRASSA. I did not reflect on the legal standing of the gentlemen who gave the judgment, but I reflected on their action in that case where they only heard one side, and then gave judgment, ignoring entirely a part of the evidence of the record.

My hon. friend shows how little he understands about these matters, and how careful he ought to be before he criticises subjects that he is not very familiar with. If he knew anything about arguing a case ex parte, he would know that when a case is argued ex parte the appellant goes to a court to some extent handicapped, because the court in such cases always argues the case for the other side. I argued one case myself before their Lordships of the Judicial Committee where the other side did not appear, and the present Attorney General of England, Sir Robert Finlay, who was the senior counsel in that case, remarked, before we went into court, that it was most unfortunate for us that there was no one on the other side, because the court, in arguing the case for the absent party, is sometimes apt to take a very strong view of the case from the standpoint of the respondent ; therefore counsel always desire the respondent to be represented rather than have to argue the case ex parte with the respondent absent.
Did you win the case ?

Yes, and it overruled a long series of decisions in Nova Scotia and two decisions of the Supreme Court of Canada, but there is not a lawyer
in the province of Nova Scotia at the present time who would be disposed to argue that the judgment of the Privy Council in that case was not a sound and correct one.

Would the hon. gentleman allow me ? As to that case of Forget and Ostigny to which he refers, I must say that the judgment of the Privy Council being an ex parte judgment has not been recognized by the judges of Quebec, because they say, and I have myself heard the Chief Justice of Quebec say in a similar case, that they cannot accept that jurisdiction because Ostigny was not represented.

Of course I am not so familiar with the rules of the hon. gentleman's province and do not know what weight is to be attached to authorities of that kind. But if he will examine the English reports during 'the last ten years, he will find the case, which I argued ex parte, to have been cited by counsel over and over again at least half a dozen times, and referred to and relied on by courts of the highest standing in England. That would simply seem to indicate that there is a different rule in different countries. It has been the rule in our own courts, and I know in the courts of England as well, to make no distinction as to the authority of such cases. The hon. member for Labelle, I think, desired to say something to me on that matter.
Mr. BOuRASSA. It is immaterial. I was going to say, that, according to the theory of my hon. friend, it would be better for a party engaging in a lawsuit to have no lawyer to plead for him.
That is treason.
I am not sure that it would not be better sometimes.
I am afraid that my hon. friend is speaking without consideration.

I think I must apologize to my hon. friend. I was about to say to the hon. member for Labelle that if he will go to the volumes of the decisions of the Supreme Court of Canada he will find many cases-I remember one from m!y own province-which have been argued ex-pnrte and in which the appellant has failed. The case of Lane vs. Macdonald from my own province was argued about twenty years ago ex-parte in the Supreme Court and the appellant failed. The court argues the case for the absent respondent and sometimes convinces itself ; and many_ lawyers, as I know, because I am speaking from experience as a( member of the bar and in that I can appeal to the hon. Minister of Justice, would rather, in the final court of apppeal. have the other side represented by counsel than to argue the case ex-parte.

What has the hon. member to say about that part of the judg-

ment of the Privy Council where they declared a fact which was directly contradicted by the evidence and based" their judgment upon it ?

I have never heard of the case to which the hon. gentleman referred until to-day. X have not examined it but I would hardly be inclined to think that so important a" part of the evidence had been overlooked by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council.
If the respondent had had a lawyer there to represent him he would have pointed that out.

That may be very true and there may have been some question overlooked. If any measure can be devised for the purpose of"eontrolling stock speculation in Canada I for one would be prepared to give it my hearty support, but I am afraid that I can hardly gather from the hon. member for Labelle 'anything that would contribute very much to that end. Stock speculation is undoubtedlv an evil, but it is an evil that, for the most part, it is almost impossible to cure bv any legislation.

Mr. Speaker, in view of what has been said on this question by the hon. member for Da-belle (Mr. Bourassa) and the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) I think I shall say a few words. I do not rise to say a woi-d against any private individual. I think we have only a right to speak of those who have inflicted an injury upon the community. I do not know whether my hon. friend from Labelle has proved his case, that an injury has been inflicted upon himself or upon others but in regard to what the hon. member for West Toronto states.
I am sure that the case he made out is correct and that is the case of the two loan companies in St. Thomas in the county which I have the honour to represent. They acted under the authority of this government in dealing in margins and they brought about perhaps the greatest calamity that has ever happened in our county. I think the attention of the government having been (Wiled to section 9 of chap. 01. they should see to it that no other companies are allowed to fall into the same condition ns that in which we now find the Atlas Loan Company and the Elgin Loan Company of St. Thomas. I know that the people there took stock in these loan companies believing that they were doing a legitimate business in loaning money on mortgages on landed property. Of course, there is very little risk in that. When I took stock" in one of these companies I believed that they were doing business in that way, but. I found that they had come to this parliament and got permission to do an illegitimate business, as I think, and the consequence is that there are widowed women, retired farmers, and

others who had made a competence for themselves who w ill be obliged to go to work again or go to the poorliouse simply because they have been fleeced of the earnings of their lifetime. I think, the government's attention having been called to this, that they should see that no other companies are allowed to engage in stock speculation as these companies have done with such disastrous results. I have nothing more to say except to express the hope that section 9 of the Act, to which I have referred, will be amended and amended this session.

Mr. Speaker, I merely wish to say that it seems to me that there is a good deal in the argument put before us by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) that we should make some effort to improve the law, and to that extent, for my own part, after what I have seen in the city of Montreal, I would be disposed to support the motion of my hon. friend. Within the last eight or ten years the fever of speculation has developed in the city of Montreal to an extent which has brought ruin to a very large number of people, to a great many families and particularly to a very large number of young men to whom it appears, as it used not to appear when I was a young man, that the best way to' obtain a suitable position in life is to acquire wealth by avoiding the observance of the law of daily work. As a rule, in the hope of acquiring wealth suddenly, they get money in any manner possible, invest that money in paying a small margin upon stock and not infrequently they are ruined and sometimes landed in the penitentiary as a result of this extraordinary tendency which is now so prevalent In Canada. I suppose it is the same in other parts of the country as it is in the city of Montreal, but I speak of Montreal more particularly because I know what is going on there. I am like the hon. member for Labelle. a man who is not given to speculation myself. I have never speculated or bought shares of any kind, but from what I have seen I am very sure that the suggestion made by the hon. member for Labelle would lie a step in the proper direction ; I refer to that part of the remedy which he proposed, that every transaction which takes place upon margin should be made more serious and more difficult by the imposition of a heavier margin. I say this with all due reservation, because I am not very conversant with these operations. I am almost sure that a law of that kind would have a great effect in the way of a deterrent from the reckless speculation which is indulged in in the city of Montreal. The provisions of chap. 42. 51 Vic. may be very good as far as they g,\ but it has not been found possible to apply section 1 to check reckless speculation and I would like to say to my hon. friend, that, being, probably, in the same situation as myself, he has lent too willing an ear

to those of this friends who have gone to the offices of brokers and lost money. He has lent too willing an ear to those who have lost money, probably through the legitimate employment by them of the firm of Mr. Forget, and the consequence of that is that my hon. friend (Mr. Bourassa) very reck-lesslv has maligned in this House this afternoon a man who in no way deserves the censure directed against him.
I have merely chosen Mr. Forget as a most striking example.
My hon. friend has been reckless in doing so, because he has very nearly coupled with Mr. Forget's name the word ' robber ' and ' despoiler of the poor.'
It was Mr. Dansereau who did that.

My hon. friend has made a mistake in quoting that controversy between Mr. Dansereau and Mr. Forget, because it was a personal matter, and we have no means of verifying what are the facts. I would say to my hon. friend (Mr. Bourassa) that he has treated with a great deal of flippancy the case of Ostigny and Forget. That was a case which interested the whole bar, and the dissent of Mr. Justice Hall was considered extremely strong, and it certainly justified the brokers of the city of Montreal-than whom I do not know a more respectable, a more honest and straight-forward and a more loyal set of men-it certainly justified them in taking the steps which they did to bring that case as far as the Privy Council My hon. friend has qualified that step, which is taken every day in the practice of our profession, as a conspiracy to wrest from the Privy Council a verdict favourable to the brokers and their alleged infamous transactions. My hon. friend (Mr. Bourassa) must be mistaken. My hon. friend knows that that case was fully discussed before the Privy Council. I have not $een the report lately, but it was considered by every member of the bar at that time to be a very strong judgment indeed, and for my own part I was impressed, as were a great many of my confreres, with the idea that the Privy Council in upholding the dissent of Mr. Justice Hall had interpreted the law as it really is in our province. I think my hon. friend from Gaspfi is mistaken in saying that our courts will not abide by the holding of the Privy Council in the case of Ostigny and Forget.
It is all a question of fact.

Yes. My hon. friend referred to the case of Roy vs. Canadian Pacific Railway. Well, in that case admissions were made which perhaps gave reason to the Privy Council in judging as it did. Very important admissions were made by my friend Mr. Gouin, who argued the case before the Privy Council, and it was upon these admissions' the Privy Council rendered judgment in the case of Roy. At any rate, I have never heard it alleged that the Privy Council made a mistake on the questions of fact as they found them in the case of Ostigny vs. Forget. My hon. friend (Mr. Bourassa) is surely mistaken in holding up to this House a man of the position of Senator Forget as one given to speculation with the object of ruining his clients-I think that is a fair interpretation of what my hon. friend (Mr. Bourassa) said. I do not mean to say that that information has not been conveyed to the hon. gentleman by parties who might have suffered in speculation.

I would not like my hon. friend to go so far as that in the interpretation of what I said. What I said was that, as the law stands now and as the practice of the brokers is, it may be that in times of a crisis they are led and almost forced to speculate against their clients. I never said that that was the object of Senator Forget or any other broker under ordinary circumstances.

I am very glad to hear my hon. friend say that, because the senator- whom I am not specially charged to defend, but who is an old friend of mine-is a man who occupies a very high position in the city of Montreal. 'He is a governor of our university, and a benefactor of that university, which stands in great need of assistance. He occupies a very high position in respect to all our philanthropic works in the city of Montreal, and I have no hesitation in saying that he generally enjoys the confidence of every class of the community. My hon. friend (Mr. Bourassa) is aware of that. I may say also that as one of our French Canadian fellow-citizens who have entered the world of finance and begun at the foot of the ladder, he has attained a position unattained previously by any of his compatriots, and which has reflected a great deal of credit, not only on himself, but on his fellow French Canadians.

Reference has been made by some of the speakers to speculation in respect to land in Manitoba and the North-west, and I wish to say a word as to that. I do not refer to any boom in Winnipeg or Toronto or any city, because lands rise and fall in value in these citie^ regularly. But I want to point out that the records of thirty years in the city of Winnipeg concerning the lands in Manitoba and the North-west show that there has been a steady increase in the price of these lands, and that there never has been any set back in that price. These records show on the average a steady increase of 12 per cent in the value of farm lands throughout Manitoba and the North-west.

I have no desire to follow the member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) through his lengthy and eloquent address, but I simply rise for the purpose of endorsing generally what he

has said. The argument has been advanced by the member for Toronto (Mr. Osier) that because some people have a tendency to do certain evil acts, there is no use in passing legislation to prevent them from committing these acts. If that argument were followed to its logical conclusion, we might as well do away with all legislation. Some people in their nature have a disposition to steal, and, per se, you should not legislate against stealing ; some people in their nature have a disposition to commit murder, and therefore, according to the logic of the hon. member (Mr. Osier), there is no use putting a law in the statute-book against murder. There are a good many people who are disposed to do immoral things, and according to the logic of the argument of the hon." member for Toronto, you should not legislate against these things. That is surely not a very logical argument, but coming from a man who is a stock broker, I am not surprised at It at all. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the member for Labelle has performed a public service in calling the attention of parliament to this evil. If it is not an evil, then there are a great many people throughout the Dominion who are labouring under a misapprehension, because there are a great many people who are under the impression that speculation on margin, as we ordinarily understand the term, is gambling pure and simple. A great many people are also under the impression that it is contrary to good morals to tolerate this spirit of gambling under the name of speculation, and they believe that parliament should provide a remedy against it. I admit that it is exceedingly difficult to stop people from speculating, but there is a wide difference between speculating in_ real estate, for example, and dealing in stocks on margin, as the term is ordinarily used. There are a good many people who have suffered from stock speculation of one kind or another, and I do think that the people of this country would welcome any legislation that would have for its object the checking of this evil. Even if such legislation does not entirely stop the unwise and improvident spirit of gambling that is abroad in the land. I was somewhat amused at the leader of the opposition, who started out apparently with the object of getting his friend from Toronto (Mr. Osier) out of the hole in which he had landed, and who. for the time being, did not admit that there was any wrong in this system of speculation, but before the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) had finished his argument, he admitted that it was an evil, and he also thought that there might be some possibility of checking it if the Minister of Justice would introduce an amendment to the Criminal Code directed against it. The hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Robinson) and the member for Toronto (Mr. Osier) both admitted the prevalence of the evil. Now, as to whether the government is or is not responsible for the speculation that was Mr. HOLMES.
carried on by the loan companies in the city of St. Thomas, that is neither here nor there. The hon. gentlemen succeed in establishing the fact that the loan companies in the city of St. Thomas were carrying on an illegal transaction in speculating in stocks, and as a result that they brought ruin and disaster on a good many families in the vicinity. These hon. gentlemen proved the contention of the hon. member from Labelle, although they did not intend to do so. If it is possible for the Minister of Justice to devote some attention to this matter, as I presume he will, by introducing an amendment to the Criminal Code, he will be doing something that will confer a great benefit on the country at large. The gambling spirit prevails to a very large extent, and whilst I admit without hesitation the impossibility of removing it entirely by legislation, I do say that we can check it to a very considerable extent. We have spent a great deal of time in this House, not only this session, but in previous sessions, in passing legislation that was vastly of less importance than the legislation which we have been invited to enact by the hon. member for Labelle.
