Mr. Speaker, when a few evenings ago I briefly referred to the subject which has been introduced this afternoon by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), I did not think that during this session it would receive as much attention from the members of this House as it has. On another occasion I may refer to the matter again, with a view to suggesting some remedy for, or some means of minimizing, the evil complained of. For that reason my remarks on this occasion shall be extremely brief. That an evil does exist has been fully demonstrated by the hon. member who has introduced the motion now in your hands.
I believe it to be a very widespread evil. We speak of the evil of intemperance ; but to my mind stock speculation brings more sorrow, more sadness, more broken hearts, more ruined homes, more suicides, than all the ravages of intemperance. We talk of the evils of the race track. Betting on the race track is nothing as compared with this evil. I have before me a quotation from the ' Canadian Sportsman ' on the subject of the worst kind of gambling. In this brief article, that paper, referring to a recent failure in the city of Toronto, says :
The class of business done by this firm has had much to do with the wild mad speculation that has had so large a number of our citizens in its grasp -within the piast year. Talk about injury being done this community by holding a race meeting conducted by gentlemen for two

weeks in the spring and one week in the autumn. There has been more citizens of Toronto ruined within the past six months and more misery caused by this carnival of reckless speculation than the Canadian turf is responsible for in the fifty years in its history.
We say, then, that it is an admitted fact that an evil does exist, and our duty here is, if possible, to find some means of minimizing that evil. The hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Osier) says that speculation has long existed and will continue to exist-that it is natural to speculate. I believe there is a great deal in that ; but that should not deter us from finding some means of minimizing what we consider an illegitimate practice. We must be careful at the same time, however, to distinguish between the broker who carries on a legitimate business, and the broker who carries on what may fairly be called an illegitimate or improper business. The business of a broker is just as legitimate and honourable as that of the banker, the merchant, or any other man engaged in the ordinary walks of life ; and no reflection to my mind should be east on that class of the community who engage in a business which is proper and legitimate and a requirement of the country. Even dealing on margin may be legitimate business. Where there is no intention to deliver the goods that are sold on margin or to implement the purchase, then I consider the business becomes a dangerous and illegitimate business. If a man has not the means to implement his purchase, he is sure to become the loser in the end, because when stocks decline, time after time, and he puts up his money until he puts up his last dollar, if he is unable to continue to meet the decline or to take over the stock which he has purchased, he must become the loser and his family will become the sufferers. I said, however, that there is a kind of dealing on margin which I consider perfectly legitimate. For example, a grain merchant of Liverpool may purchase a million bushels of wheat in New York. Knowing that he has a sufficient margin between the price he pays for that wheat in New York and the price he expects to obtain for it in [DOT]Liverpool, provided there is no decline in price in the meantime, it is perfectly legitimate for him to sell short the million bushels, and so protect himself against loss. That is the kind of transaction that is engaged in every day of the year. That man has the goods to deliver, because he has purchased the wheat in New York, and is able to implement the transaction.
I remember very well when the Bill referred to by the hon. member for Labelle was introduced into this House by Sir John Thompson, I believe it was first introduced in the Senate by Sir John Abbott, then Prime Minister of Canada. That Bill was aimed against the small bucket shops which at that time were all through the country 221
doing a large business. It was not intended to operate against the legitimate broker at all. However, means were very soon found of evading that law, simply by changing the base of operations. Instead of consummating the transaction say in Toronto or Montreal, the broker simply wires the deal to New York or Buffalo, so as to have it completed outside of the country, and not commit an offence against the laws of Canada.
Dealing on margin no doubt makes speculation easy, because it is done with less money than would be required if a man were buying stocks and paying the full price for them. To my mind what we must keep in view in discussing this matter is the means by which we can make it more difficult to speculate on margin. I believe that if we can limit the supply of money which the broker controls and which he obtains on the security of the stocks he holds, then we will limit the operations of the broker, and minimize to a very large extent the dealings on margin. It has been suggested that it would be a good thing to license the broker. I would not approve of that. If you license a broker to do this class of busines, you simply make the business more respectable, and create an injury rather than a benefit. To my mind the business at the present time is too respectable. It has been transferred from the small bucket shop to the large broker's office, which at the present time is practically nothing more nor less than a big respectable bucket shop.

Mr. Speaker, unlimited stock speculation is damaging to the country in many ways. It limits the amount of money available for the legitimate business of the country. That lias been proven over and over again. The money of the country that ought to be reserved for the legitimate business of the country is often sent out of the country to be used for stock speculation. The proof of that is apparent to-day. We have the most prosperous times probably that ever existed in the history of the continent of America ; but by reason of inflated companies, by reason of millions of stock being put on the market, that stock has not been digested, as the term is, and the result is that in the midst of this great prosperity there are many people labouring under financial difficulties brought on by stock speculation. Then, stock speculation is a danger to the loan companies and the insurance companies, the reserves of which sometimes find their way into the stock market. Other great interests are involved in that way. The loan companies have had the public faith in them largely reduced, and the time has arrived when this parliament should do something to prevent their investing the money of their depositors and shareholders- in some cases to the extent of ninety per



cent-in stock speculation and only ten per cent paid in advances on real estate, which is the purpose for which they were specially created. It is said that we cannot make a cure, but I believe some kind of a cure may be effected on the lines laid clown by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) this afternoon and the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) this evening. It is all right for men who have the money to go into stock speculation. People talk about betting on horse racing, but there is this to be said in its favour as against stock gambling, that when a man puts up his money on a horse, he knows how much he stands to lose, but when a man puts up his money on stocks on margin, he never knows how much more he will have to pay and what obligations are ahead of him. If some law could be passed whereby the amount of margin would be increased or which would prevent loan companies from advancing more than a certain percentage on speculative stocks, the evil would be largely reduced. A strong case has been made out, and I think it is incumbent on the government to introduce some kind of legislation in the way of curtailing the power which the loan companies have of lending money on stocks.

(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) has rendered, and will render a valuable service to the public generally, and to several people in particular, by presenting the motion put in your hands this afternoon. The hon. member merely stated aloud what every one in this country has been whispering for several mouths past: that there exists a system of speculation on margin of a most fraudulent character ; a system of speculation which is the more dangerous because it is apparently carried on under the cover of our statutory law of 1888. The facts on which my hon. friend for Labelle has based his argument have not been contradicted by any of the members who addressed the House, either on this side or on the opposite. Indeed, they are taken from the records of two cases looked upon as very famous and which were even taken to his Majesty's Privy Council in appeal. The facts referred to by my hon. friend and which are undeniable aud uucontradicted, are recounted in those cases.
My hon. friend also referred to certain facts in connection with the famous controversy which arose in the months of September and October last between Messrs. Dan-sereau and Forget. The hon. member for Labelle in pointing out with the eloquence and ability which we all recognize, the facts connected with this controversy, showed, I think, that fraud very often enters in these speculations which lie denounced.
The hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) complained that the hon. member for Labelle had repeated some statements iii which mention was made of thieves and Mr. MACLEAN.
swindlers, because these expressions seemed to apply to Mr. Forget. It appears to me we should not be afraid of calling certain things by their name, and particularly of calling a thief a thief. When certain doings are recognized by us as bad, I do not see any reason why we should object to designating as they deserve those who are guilty of them. However, according to the hon. member for Jacques Cartier, my hon. friend from Labelle had no right to qualify as he did the conduct of those who commit those acts considered as actual frauds.
I think the hon. member for Labelle might have gone a little further than he has done, in giving out certain facts in connection with this Dansereau-Forget dispute. For instance, if he had carried his inquiry a little further, he might have informed the House of the famous circumstance of the decease of the well-known broker, which Mr. Forget availed himself of to refuse paying to his client Dausereau what he owed him. I think the hon. member for Jacques Cartier would not object to our calling a robber he who actually robs his client.

(Translation.) I think the hon. member is going a little too far. Rule 13 of the Rules and Regulations reads as follows :
No member shall use offensive words aga'.us: either House, or against any member thereof.

(Translation.) I was going to say, Mr. Speaker, when you called my attention to the rule, that the facts elicited by my remarks had taken place before Mr. Forget was a senator. That was the explanation which I proposed giving to the House. In any case I bow humbly to your ruling.
Every one admits that the facts elicited by that famous dispute are true. It is stated that after all the evil is not so great, since two cases only have been found where fraud was apparent. As a matter of fact nobody is very willing to admit having practised that kind of speculation, whether he has succeeded or not. That reminds me of Sir Charles Tupper's answer to the inquiry as to how he had made his fortune. The ex leader of the Conservative party, instead of admitting that he had speculated, merely stated that he had practised as a physician for three, four or five years, and in that way had amassed the immense wealth he possessed at the time.
If those who profit by speculation are in no way anxious to boast of the means whereby they have succeeded, the more so are the losers in the game reticent in this connection. The evil is much more widespread than seemed to think those who spoke after the hon. member for Labelle, and who, while not controverting the argument brought forward by this gentleman, seemingly claimed that it is not expedient to introduce a law regulating speculation on stock in this country.

The contrary is to my knowledge, Mr. Speaker. I have received letters from friends urging the necessity of a law that would protect these poor victims ; and here are the very words which one of them uses :
* To protect those who are foolish enough to do as I have done.'
It is evident that those who speculate on margin (I mean those who have only a few hundred or a few thousand dollars) are induced to do so by the advice of those who, certainly, control the rise or fall of stock in most cases and thus rapidly build up a fortune for themselves at the expense of the buyers.
The evil exists, and the fact having been brought to the attention of parliament, it seems that the Minister of Justice aud the government should find a means, not of interfering with legitimate speculation, but of putting a stop to that abusive speculation which leads these poor victims to the consequences we know.
I said a moment ago that those who do not succeed are far from being boastful of a practice which has caused their ruin ; and so, we are not made aware of the extent of the evil. But we all know, it is notorious to-day, that even professional men, notaries, Jiave been sent to the penitentiary merely because they had speculated with money put in their hands by individuals, often poor widows, who had only a few hundred dollars savings. These notaries had committed these frauds in an endeavour to meet the calls made on them to cover their margin on account of a sudden rise or fall of the stock, which they had been unable to foresee. In the same way bank cashiers have been obliged to quit the country because they could not refund the money which they had embezzled for purposes of speculation.
It suffices to mention these facts without giving names or entering into particulars, to show that the evil exists. Now, that evil having been brought to the attention of the House, it is its duty, as well as that of the government to try and find a remedy.
In conclusion, I wish to thank once more my hon. friend from T.abelle for having brought up that question. I think he has thereby rendered a great service to the public. The almost unanimous expression of opinion on the part of the members, who admitted that the evil existed, should induce the government, and more especially the Minister of Justice to take proper measures for remedying it.

I concur very heartily, Mr. Speaker, in the remarks made by the hon. member for
Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) and my hon. friend from Napierville (Mr. Monet) as regards this great evil. I have listened very attentively to that strong indictment made against gambling and what I may term gambling dens, established in our large cities. In my opinion, my hon. friend from Labelle has rendered' this country 2214
a real service, and I hope his speech will be read by all the young men just about entering on their career in this country. It has been my lot to represent in the district of Montreal-the largest judicial district of the province of Quebec and perhaps the largest in the whole Dominion-the Crown in my official capacity of Crown Prosecutor. I have seen, term after term, young men belonging to the notarial profession, for instance, standing indicted for forgery and fraud-for having taken the money which had been deposited with them by clients; and the cause of their being arrested and sent to the penitentiary was this passion to gamble on the stock exchange, even if they had to do it with money which did not belong to them. That is one of the saddest chapters of criminal history in Canada. I have witnessed such cases often, and therefore I can bear testimony to the truth of the picture presented by my hon. friend from Labelle. What does the hon. gentleman propose ? The remedy seems very simple, raise the margin. Go into the city of Montreal or anywhere else, where the stock exchange reigns supreme, and you will be told by young lawyers, notaries, and clerks, that they go to the brokers offices just as they would go to a club to play a game of cards or to a lottery. We have legislated against lotteries because they are based on chance. Why should we not legislate for the same reason against the stock exchange ? The young man with a salary of $500, or even with a salary of $1,000 per year, who goes to a broker and buys shares of say Dominion Iron and Steel or any other stock on a margin of five, ten or fifteen per cent, is nothing else, to my mind, but a common gambler : and if you would raise this margin to twenty-five per cent you will do the young men of this country the best service you can render them. This debate should be a great moral lesson to our young men. I am told by the hon. member for St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) that it is better to preach by example, which is no doubt true, but unfortunately the best educated men of this country are addicted to that gambling frenzy. When men lose at the stock exchange, they accuse the fiscal policy of the government as the cause of their losses. Lately we have heard of many thousands of the young men of this country losing money through speculating in stocks, and the government was charged with being the cause of those losses. Well, is it not a fact that the real cause was the depression brought about by the stock brokers themselves ? I believe that the depression was due to their own quarrels, as we have been told this afternoon. I would urge the adoption of this resolution; indeed, this debate will furnish a highly moral lesson, which I hope will bear fruit.

That there is urgent need of legislation to pre-

vent stock gambling, if you can prevent by legislation, no one will deny. But tbe question is what could you do by legislation to prevent it ? I think that the most effective remedy would be to compel actual transfer and registration at the time a sale of stock is made. X have always thought that every stock broker should have the stock on hand before selling it, and when he sells it, he should immediately put the sale on record and transfer the stock. Monthly returns should be sent the government of actual transactions; and if it be found that a broker has been dealing with stocks not in his possession, he should be punished by a fine. To sell stocks short or stocks which you do not own should be made a punishable offence.
This will pretty effectually stop it, so far as I know. Now, it may be said that the variety of stocks is so great that this could not be done. When stocks are listed they become, in a measure, public property. At least, they are negotiable property and it is an easy matter to take record of them. Stock brokers do not deal in wild-cat schemes, mining speculations and stock of that kind. They handle stocks for which there is a public demand or stocks which have intrinsic value. If a stock broker takes the responsibility of handling stocks at all the first requisite should be that the stock should be registered. Then, a record should be kept of every transaction and a return made somewhat similar to the return made by the banks, so that the government could trace the stock, know whether the broker was dealing on margin or selling something that he did not own. If the transactions were confined to bona fide purchases and sales, it seems to me, not so much harm would be done. I believe that probably it would be an additional safety to compel a purchaser to put up a larger margin. Many deal in stocks on a small margin who would not touch them if the margin were greater. I am not so pronounced on that point as I am in believing that every stock transaction should be registered and that there should be a monthly return of every broker who deals in stocks, and, if it is shown that he is dealing in stocks he does not own. he should be fined.
The ? MINISTER OF JUSTICE (Hon. Charles Fitzpatrick). I believe that the question raised by the motion of my hon. friend from La belle (Mr. Bourassa) is one well worthy the consideration of this House. I have listened patiently and carefully to all that has been said in order that I might gather suggestions that would be useful in any effort I may make to remedy the grievances which exist. My hon. friend (Mr. Bourassa) must bear in mind that this question is one over which we have only a partial control. A transaction in stocks is more a matter of civil contract which is to be regulated, to a large extent, by the law of the Mr. SPROULE.
particular province in which the transaction takes place.
Who gives the stock broker authority to carry on his business ?

That is a matter of local concern. We can only deal with that question here so far as we may make the dealing in stocks a penal offence. I agree with all that has been said about the evils that have resulted from stock gambling transactions. L have in my own experience known of cases of the greatest possible hardship. I am quite within the limits of what I know to be absolutely accurate, when I say that the Yille Marie Bank of Montreal was wrecked as the result of! stock gambling engaged in by persons connected with the bank. I have known cases of young men engaged in banks-I have one before my mind now-a young man who took $40,000 of the bank's money in one month for the purpose of stock gambling. I know a case which resulted in suicide. These are very serious and real evils, evils for which we feel there ought to be some remedy. Yet it is very easy to say that we ought to stop these things. Before we take any action it is better to carefully and accurately consider the method to be adopted to arrive at the end we all have in view. It is idle to call all stock brokers villians and scoundrels. I listened carefully to what was said by my hon. friend (Mr. Bourassa) and I am sure that he did not use a word that could be construed into a wish to apply such terms to all the members of a respectable calling in the community. All who have had experience in affairs know1 that stock brokers are as respectable as any other class and as well deserving of our consideration. All stock dealing is not criminal ; all stock dealing is not improper ; all stock dealing is not to be discouraged. A man knows of a stock he thinks is likely to rise. He goes to a broker and asks him to buy a hundred shares of that stock. The broker says : I will buy the stock, and yoxi will give me ten, fifteen or twenty per cent margin. The broker purchases the stock ; but, to do so, he must pay the then market value and must supplement the amount advanced by the client by borrowing or advancing the balance of the purchase price. If he charges a commission for this service there is nothing wrong about the transaction, nothing even to be discouraged. He makes the purchase, registers the stock in the name of the client, if the client pays in full, or, if not. he registers it in his own name and becomes responsible to the bank that makes the advance. No doubt, he transfers the shares to the bank as collateral security for the advance. In case the broker pledges his own credit, in addition to the security, to the bank for the purpose of getting that advance to accommodate his client. There is nothing wrong in all this, nothing to

cause us to condemn all stock brokers' transactions. But that which is wrong, that which is to be condemned, that for which we should endeavour to find a remedy, is the case of a man who goes to a so-called stock broker-because these people are not worthy of the name of brokers-and goes through the form of purchasing so many shares when he and the broker with whom he deals knows that there is no intention on the part of the broker to buy a share of the stock, much less to transfer it to his client. In such a case the client simply puts up a certain amount of money for margin ; if the stock rises, the difference between the then current price of the stock and the rise, in addition to the margin, goes to the credit of the client. If there is a decline in the price, then, of course, if it is sufficient, the client, loses his margin. That sort of stock brokerage illustrates the old rule, ' heads I win, tales you lose.-the broker being the man in the position of advantage. If we can reach that form of gambling-for it is nothing else- we shall go far to bring about a remedy for the evils pointed out. I have not considered the matter very carefully, but it appears to me that the statute my hon. friend (Mr. Bourassat referred to this afternoon would go far in the way of remedying the evil, if it had not been amended after it came back from the Senate. That statute to which my hon. friend referred is a part of onr Criminal Code. That article provides :
Every one is guilty of any indictable offence and liable to five years' imprisonment, and to a fine of five hundred dollars, who, with the intent to make gain or profit by the rise or fall in price of any stock of any incorporated or unincorporated company or undertaking, either in Canada or elsewhere or of any goods, wares or merchandise-
(a.) Without the bona fide intention of acquiring any such shares.
But here is the apparently harmless amendment that was made to Abbott s Bill when it came back from the Senate, and which I think makes the whole section inoperative :
But it is not an offence if the broker of t.he purchaser receives delivery, on his behalf-
-remember, it is the broker who takes delivery-
__of the article sold, notwithstanding that such
broker retains or pledges the same as security for the advance of the purchase money or any part thereof.
As was pointed out by the member for Labelie, a broker may have five different clients, each of whom purchases say 500 shares, and he, the broker, may only own 500 shares, he can use these shares so as to evade responsibility if proceeded against under the Criminal Code notwithstanding that with respect to the 2,000 shares the transaction is a mere gamble, and against such transactions we should legislate if
possible. But before applying a remedy we must find out the nature of the disease, then after a little consideration no doubt we will find some kind of a remedy for the disease.
I would like, before sitting down, to make a reference to what was said this afternoon about the case of Forget and Ostigny. I think the hon. member for La-belle went a little too far in his criticisms of their Lordships of the Privy Council. The Forget and Ostigny case was merely one of fact. The question was as to whether a particular contract they were called upon to consider was a gaming contract within the meaning of an article of the civil code of our province. Three judges of the lower court held that, as a matter of fact, it was not, while their Lordships of the Privy Council held as a matter of fact that it was, reversing the decision of the lower court and holding that it was a gambling transaction. That was a question upon which men may differ. I would like to say this, that I consider the right of appeal to the Privy Council as a great safeguard to the people of this country, and to the province of Quebec in particular. The Privy Council are far away from our little local troubles and difficulties; they are men of broad instincts, men of great learning, aud I think I may say, if the hon. member for Labelie will permit me, speaking of one who has passed away, that one of the greatest civil law lawyers I ever knew was a member of the Privy Council, Lord Watson. He had been trained in the law of Scotland, which is to a large extent based upon the same principles as our law in the province of Quebec. He knew his civil law thoroughly. I remember having myself heard him correct a quotation from Pothier that was made by a lawyer from our province, and he corrected him in such a way as to indicate not only that he knew Pothier, but what is far better, that he understood him. Now, there are other great lawyers, Lord Davy, for instance, who also knows something about our civil law, and who is certainly one of the best Roman law lawyers living at present within the limits of the British empire; and a man who knows his Roman law has a very good foundation for the civil law in our province. Let us not be too prone in criticism of the Privy Council. I have been before them, and I know that they care very little about the petty differences and difficulties that trouble us in this country. Their only desii'e is to do what is just and fair. They have got the capacity, they have got the learning, and they have got the desire to do what is fair and just. I may conclude by saying that I think the hon. member for Labelie has drawn our attention to a grievance, to a grievance that requires a remedy. I cannot say that I can do much for him at the present time, but insofar as my limited knowledge and experience go, I am entirely at his service, and I shall en-

deavour, so far as possible to find a remedy for the grievance he has suggested. But I must ask him, if he will permit me, to withdraw his motion.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. I. TARTE (Montreal, St. Mary's).
speechtext:
Several lion, gentlemen who have addressed the House have taught a lesson to the young men of this country. They told them that they ought not to gamble. I quite agree with the advice that has been tendered to the young generation; but knowing what I know, and what is well known in this House and outside of this House, I think we should begin our education of the young generation by setting them an example. When Ministers of the Crown, both in this parliament and in local legislatures, when members of parliament, when secretaries of ministers, when men who pretend to know every thing, that is going on, gamble and buy stocks right and left, it is not surprising that young lawyers and young clerks gamble and speculate. I say it again, when members of parliament, when ministers, not one, but several of them-X do not make any personal allusion, I speak of ministers generally of the various parliaments of this country-are known to gamble and speculate, we must not be surprised if the younger generation follow that dangerous example. Let us give the example ourselves. My hon. friend from Gaspf: (Mr. Lemieux) alluded to the case of steel and coal. Well, we have heard very little else but steel and coal during last session of parliament. We could not walk through the lobbies of this House without hearing steel and coal. Everybody was buying. It was not the young men alone who were guilty of gambling, it was men in high positions who were buying stock. My hon. friend will permit me to tell him that gambling is one thing and tariff is another thing. The tariff was not sufficient in the case of steel and iron, and the best evidence that it was not sufficient is the fact that a free trader like my hon. friend the Minister of Finance has at last made up his mind to give additional bounties to that industry. Surely if the Minister of Finance was convinced that the tariff is high enough, he would not for the sake of gamblers, add probably $1,000,000 to the Budget of Canada. Let us deal with gamblers, but let us not mix up tariff matters in a question of this kind. Again I say. and I think I am expressing the sentiment of all those who know what is going on, that it will not be sufficient for us to enact laws here while men in high positions give a bad example by gambling and buying stock *with which parliament may have to deal. I think that is a very improper thing indeed. I do not wish to give lessons to anybody, that is not by any means my intention. But I think it is a very improper thing for members of parliament and ministers to gamble in stocks of corporations that sooner or later may apply to this parlia-Hon. Mr. FITZPATRICK.
rnent for favours in the shape of additional duties and bounties.

In view of the fact that the city I represent is one of the greatest sufferers in the Dominion of Canada from stock speculation, I feel I would fail in my duty if I were to remain silent on this question which is now before the House. The papers of this country have been tilled for weeks with news concerning the unfortunate calamity which occurred in connection with some of the loan companies in the city of St. Thomas. I can testify that a gentleman who was looked upon as a pillar of the church has confessed that he has been not only taking the people's money, but he has committed forgery, theft and fraud. So, while there may be very little sympathy for the gentlemen whom the hon. member for St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) referred to, ministers and members of parliament and business men who indulge in stock speculation, there can be a great deal of sympathy for the poorer classes of the people who have saved up small earnings and then, induced by a broker or a manager of a loan company, have engaged in stock speculation and lost all their money.
I trust that the hon. Minister of Justice, who has announced that he proposes to take this matter in hand, will be successful in meeting the case that I have pointed out, namely, protecting the small depositors or those who have been induced to go into speculation in stocks. But, I think he will find it is a somewhat difficult task when he undertakes to check hazardous speculation. If I desired to enter into a hazardous speculation, or if I desired to enter into what I thought was a good speculation, and which turned out to be a poor or hazardous speculation, I think I could get over the difficulty. I could buy stocks in New York or Chicago, and I do not see how we could by legislation passed in this House prevent a person from indulging in speculation in stocks in the United States. Perhaps there may be some method known to the hon. minister for overcoming that difficulty, but as far as I can see there will be a great deal of difficulty in framing legislation to entirely wipe out speculation in hazardous stocks. A year ago in my own city not only old men, but young men, married women and young women indulged in speculation in stocks. Many of them made quite large sums of money, but when the slump came they not only lost all the profits they had made, but they lost the savings of many years previous to that. Iam glad to take part in this discussion. I have been asked on many occasions since the misfortunes occurred to the loan companies in St. Thomas by people who lost their money if legislation to prevent a recurrence of such a disaster could not be passed by this House,

and I shall be glad to lend my assistance when the occasion arises.

With the indulgence of the House and in reply to the statement made by the lion. Minister of Justice, I would like to say that I did not bring this motion in with the idea that legislation ought to be enacted this session, but I brought the question up so as to cause a discussion to be had in this House, and so as to get the hon. Minister of Justice at work on the matter. The hon. Minister of Justice has expressed his willingness to do something, but I would like to get from him a clearer expression of opinion. Of course, I understand that the question has to be carefully studied, not only from a legal point of view, but from a financial point of view as well. I quite understand that my hon. friend will have to put himself into communication with bankers and financial men throughout the country, and if he is prepared to do that so as to be able next session to bring in some legislation on the matter, I am willing to accept that.

There will be this session some amendments to the law resxiecting loan companies. I have had occasion to prepare some amendments that will probably be introduced by the hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding). In respect to the amendments which are necessary to meet the grievances pointed out by the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), I will endeavour as far as possible to introduce such amendments as will meet the difficulty. Of course, it will be necessary to make inquiry, because, with all due deference and respect for the hon. member for Montreal, St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte), I have not that practical experience which comes from actually dealing 'in stocks.
I have not either.

I am absolutely guiltless in that respect, whatever my other iniquities may be. The short road to fortune has never had any attraction for me, and I think the same thing is true of my colleagues in the government.	*
Amendment (Mr. Bourassa) withdrawn, motion agreed to, and House went into Committee of Supply.
Census, $35,000.
What time do you expect to elapse before the census is completed ? I understand you have dismissed a number of employees who were engaged on the staff. How many do you still retain ?

It is hoped the work will be'finished before the New Year, and
possibly earlier than that, but certainly by that time. We were able to dispense with the service of 35 or 40 clerks on the 1st of July. There are between 60 and 70 left still in the office at work, and we expect that they will finish the work about the new year or possibly the 1st of December.
speakername: The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Hon. Svdney Fisher).

speechtext: Would the hon. minister tell us, now that he is within measure-able distance of the end, what is going to be the whole cost of the census ?

I have already placed a statement before the House of what the cost was up to a recent date, and I think it was $1,100,000. This vote ought to finish it. That would make it about $1,150,000. I am speaking from memory, but a statement was made to the House some time ago in answer to a question.

I understand that after the instructions had been issued to the enumerators a further supplementary circular was issued to the enumerators in the province of Ontario. Wrould the hon. minister make a statement about that and would he produce a copy of the circular ?
There was one error in the instructions, but immediately after they were sent out, and before the work of enumeration commenced, the correction of that error was sent to the commissioners.
Does the minister say that that did not increase the cost of the census?
I do not think it increased it beyond the expenses of the messages that were sent to the commissioners.
Has the minister settled with the malcontents among the enumerators who claimed they should receive more pay. Did he give them all they claimed ?

On the contrary, there was a good deal of dissatisfaction in consequence of their not receiving what they demanded. They were paid according to the schedule rates which were issued with the instructions.
WTere they satisfied with that ?
I dare say a good many of them were not satisfied when they did not receive all they asked for.
Did the Minister of Agriculture call to his assistance the Minister of Labour to settle the dispute ?
No.

I read the instructions carefully, and I must say that it was easy for one to come to the conclusion that the rate of pay was to be $3 per day. I do not think they would have much difficulty in upholding that contention in a court of law. The instructions said that they were to do so much work for which they were to be paid, not to exceed $3 per day, and the natural inference was that they would get $3 per day.
That was preceded by the distinct statement that they were to be paid at schedule rates.
What remuneration was paid to Mr. Drolet, who had charge of the census in relation to the industries and manufactures in Montreal ?
I am informed that he was paid at the rate of $125 a month.
How many months did he devote to that work ?
I am informed that he was at work about eight months.
Had he any assistants ?

He had enumerators under him who took the details in each locality ; he having the general supervision and being responsible for their management. He had three in Montreal and others in different parts of the province.
There is no doubt that $125 per month was the exact amount of his remuneration ?
That was his pay, but he had travelling expenses when he went about the province.
Did the census officers employ any lawyers in the city of Montreal, and if so what was the amount paid to those lawyers ?
I am informed that through the Department of Justice a case was taken out against a manufacturer who refused to give some information required in the census.
Who was the lawyer, and what was the amount of remuneration paid him ?

I understand it was Mr. Wilfrid Mercier, who is in charge of the law business there for the Department of Justice. I cannot say what remuneration was paid him, but I presume the costs were taxed in the ordinary way by the Department of Justice.

Will the minister ascertain before another meeting of the committee Hon. Mr. FISHER.
what was the exact amouht paid to Mr. Mercier ?

Last session the minister stated that one of the causes of the increase of expenditure for taking this census as compared with the census of 1891, was that the enumerators and commissioners had a greater number of schedules to fill out this census than last. Was that a correct understanding of the matter ?

Not quite. The statement made was that there were a very much larger number of questions to be answered. The word ' schedule ' is rather an indefinite word used in that way. A schedule as meant in the census, is a sheet on which are the questions across the top of the columns and down the side a space for the names of the individuals who are enumerated. Opposite the name of each individual the questions are to be filled in. This is the schedule, but a schedule may have five questions or fifty on it, and it may have ten names or fifty names of persons enumerated. The statement that there are so many schedules in the one census or so many schedules in another census is no measure of comparison between the work of the two censuses.

The other day I asked the minister, how many schedules were filled in either in whole or in part by census enumerators in the counties of Halton, Cardwell and Peel in 1891. The hon. minister gave this :	Halton, 1,724 ; Cardwell,
1,221 ; Peel, 1,215. Do I understand from the minister now that this does not include all the work to be found on the schedules given to the enumerators in these counties?

No. My hon. friend misunderstands me. What I mean is that a comparison of the schedules of 1901 with the schedules of 1891 is no indication of the amount of work done in the filling in of the schedules by the enumerators. The answers given to the hon. gentleman's question were correct as given. The hon. gentleman asked how many schedules there were, that is, how many sheets. The answer gives the number, but it does not tell how many questions or how many persons' names there were on each schedule, and without having these numbers a comparison between the number of schedules is no measure of the amount of work done respectively in the two censuses.
In so far as the schedules are concerned. If I understand the hon. minister correctly, the enumerators in those counties did more work in 1891 than thev did in 1901.
No.

Well, let me read the hon. minister's answer to the two questions I put to him this session. The first was : What

were the entries in the schedules in 1891 and in 1901 ? The answer was that in 1891 there were 651 more in Halton, 430 more in Cardwell and 374 more in Peel. What I mean to say is that in so far as the schedules are concerned, the enumerators in those three counties did more work in 1891 than in 1901. There is no question about that.
Yes, there is every question about that. My kon. friend's inference from a comparison of the number of schedules, that in 1891 the enumerators did more work than in 1901 is not a correct inference.
In so far as the schedules are concerned ?

In so far as the schedules are concerned it is not a correct inference, because, as a matter of fact, the schedule in 1891 only had 25 names upon it, whereas the schedule in 1901 had 50, that is to say, with every line of the schedule filled ; and there was an answer by every one of these fifty names to every question across the top of the schedule ; and in many instances the schedules in 1891 had not as many questions across the top as the schedules in 1901. Therefore, when my hon. friend counts the number of schedules used by the enumerators in 1891 and compares it with the number used by the enumerators in 1901, the comparison is of absolutely no use to show the amount of work done by the enumerator. You require to have, not only the number of schedules, but the number of questions on each schedule and the number of names entered on each ; and then, by working the matter out arithmetically, you will get a true comparison of the work.

I am anxious to understand this matter. I took these three counties for the reason that their population is very much less in 1901 than it was in 1891. For instance, in the county of Peel there were mdre than 1,700 people less, though the territory is exactly the same, and I am quite sure there are no more manufacturing establishments. Therefore, it is difficult for me to undertand why it cost nearly double the amount to take the census in 1901 than it did in 1891, and I asked these questions for the purpose of getting the information. If the answers do not afford a fair comparison, would it be too much to ask the hon. minister to lay on the Table a statement of the questions asked by the enumerators in 1901 and the questions asked in 1891, so that a fair comparison may be made ?

As I said a moment ago, when these questions were asked I knew that the answers would not give a fair criterion of the work done, and I therefore had a statement made out. which shows that for these three counties the number of forms of schedules in
the census of 1891 was 9 and in the census of 1901 15. But on the 9 forms of schedules used in 1891 there were 216 different questions, while on the 15 different forms of schedules used in 1901 there were 657 different questions, or over three times as many. The number of schedules is no indication of the amount of work. I have here a statement of the questions put by the enumerators and the answers taken down. In the census of 1891, the number of questions put and answers recorded was 2,111,136. In the census of 1901 it was 3,034,529, or practically half as many more.
Then that would make a half as much more work in 1901 as in 1891.
In so far as the questions and answers are concerned.
Would you regard that as half as much more work ?
Practically.
Would it not be fair to say that it might be one-quarter as much more work ? It would hardly be one-half as much more to answer a few questions.
When you take everything into consideration, you can take it fairly as half as much more.
But it costs the government more than double to do half as much more work.
In 1891 Canada was in a period of depression and labour was plentiful and cheap, whereas In 1901 the country was prosperous and labour was scarce and dear.

In the Public Accounts' Committee, the hon. gentleman's officers refused to bring down the schedules on the ground that they were private. The committee wanted to examine those schedules in order to determine whether certain suspicions were well-founded, which they had entertained regarding the taking of the census. I am not sure that there was an absolute refusal.

That question has been threshed out on various occasions, especially in connection with the census of 1881 and 1891 ; and while it was held that the names of the individuals were not private and confidential, the details of the schedules were considered absolutely so and were to be kept secret. Under these circumstances. I had nothing to do but to refuse to allow the schedules to be made public.

I would like to ask by what right the minister refused to allow these to come before the committee. The or-

der of reference was for all the documents, and I do not see by' what authority the hon. gentleman set aside that order.
I told my officers that I would take the responsibility on myself of not allowing these schedules to be brought before the committee.
Where is the rule which gives the hon. gentleman that authority to control the committee ?
I did not undertake to control the committee. What I did was to control my officers and I take the responsibility.
Under what rule ?
None is required. A minister is responsible for the work of his department.

To my mind, the minister has taken on himself an authority which is not justified by any rule. His officers are before the committee and in its hands and not in the hands of the minister. It was an improper interference on his part with the rights of the committee to prevent the committee being put in possession of documents ordered by the House. If it is essentially necessary that these papers should be examined in secret, the House can appoint a special committee to examine them, but the minister has no right to dictate to the committee what its duties are.

The hon. minister takes a very strange position. He admits that he gave an order to his officers not to produce certain papers, which the committee had ordered, and says that he is responsible to the committee and parliament. When called to account, the hon. gentleman refuses to give any reasons, but admits his responsibility. For, what my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) has done is exactly to call the minister to account under the rule of responsibility and ask him by what authority he forbade the officer of the 'department to produce those papers. The minister says : I did give the order, and am responsible to the House : and he gives no other reason for the arbitrary exercise of his authority. It seems to me. he does not admit his responsibility at all.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) lias entirely ignored the explanation I gave a few minutes ago. I said that this very question of the secrecy of the schedules had been threshed out certainly on one memorable occasion in this House in connection with the census of 1891, and I think a similar discussion took place in connection with the census of 1881. On each of these occasions, the minister in charge took the position that I take now, and the House supported and endorsed the minister. I do Mr. SPROULE.
not remember the exact procedure. But I recollect the fact, and I am acting upon that precedent. I say that this course has been taken by previous Ministers of Agriculture, and that it has been approved by the Commons of Canada. I believe it to be the right course. My hon. friend knows that, under the rules of the House he has the means of calling me to account by bringing up the matter for discussion and moving for my condemnation. I am willing to face that responsibility.

I have no remembrance of such a discussion as the hon. minister refers to. It may have taken place, and I not remember. But my view of the duties and authority of the committee leads me to the conclusion that such a position as that taken by the minister would be wrong ; and the fact that the House had declared to the contrary would not change my opinion. As I understand it, all papers and documents relating to matters of public expenditure to be inquired into by the committee the committee may call for. If the committe has not authority to compel the production of them, it asks authority of the House, and that authority is invariably given so far as my memory goes. I know of no rule in Bourinot, May or any other parliamentary authority which justifies the contention of the minister. It is true that a vote of the House would be regarded as a precedent and would probably be held as justification for action on similar lines by the minister. But, as I say, I have no re-memberance of any such vote. I have not had time to look the matter up. I read of this affair in the newspapers when I was on the road. I thought it a most extraordinary proceeding, and decided to bring up the question in the House. I intended to look into the matter before doing so, but have not had time. I am quite clear in the opinion that the committee should not be hampered in its work of inquiring into transactions involving the expenditure of the peoples' money.

As the minister has taken a definite attitude, and as he must realize that this is an important question, no doubt he has fortified himself with precedents. Surely the hon. gentleman will go a little further than he has done, and will satisfy the committee, at least to the extent of referring us to the authority lie relies upon, so that we may ascertain, as a matter of fact, that the same point was involved in previous discussions as was involved in this one. I think this is a reasonable request.

I have not examined the matter in the way my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) indicates, I do know that there was the debate I referred to in connection with the census of 1S9L In fact, I think debates took place

on several occasions on this point. Hon. gentlemen then in opposition inquired with regard to certain points of the census of 1891, and demanded that certain information should he given. The lion. Minister of Agriculture of that time, thinking that this would involve the disclosure of the details of the schedules, would not give the information. I cannot say at the moment whether there was a vote or whether the position of the minister wras approved simply by the matter being dropped. I remember that the position was taken that the list of names or anything of that kind should be disclosed, but business details, particulars with regard to families or property, were to be held secret and inviolate. And that was quite understandable and proper. The questions of the census are more or less inquisitorial. My hou. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) referred to a law case where a manufacturing firm in Montreal contended that they were not bound to give the details of their business. The Census Act required them to give details, but the condition is that these shall be held secret and confidential. Only on that condition are we allowed to exact the information. When the compilation takes place in the census tables, the totals and general results are given, but nobody knows the business details. On that occasion the leaders of hon. gentlemen opposite formed the government, and the position they took is the one I now take. I believe that they were right, and that they followed the spirit and the letter of the Census Act and that any departure from the rule they laid down would be contrary to the law. I do not propose to act contrary to the law if I can help it.

I cannot say 'that the explanation of the minister is satisfactory to myself. In the first place, the holding he speaks of seems to have been before he took office, and there has been no holding of that kind since. I understood the hon. gentleman to say that he himself had previously taken that position, and the House had exonerated him. But it seems, from what he says, that that is not the case. The question that was 'decided rose under a previous administration. For my own part, I cannot bring myself to agree with the minister on the merits of the question. The minister is not able to invoke any rule under which he was at liberty to refuse to the committee the information which the committee sought, except this vague precedent of a previous administration. He is aware that the members of the committee have a right of access to these documents as well as the minister himself. The meetings of the committee are private, and the public is excluded theoretically from its meetings; but as members of this House we are just as much entitled to take communication of these private schedules, under
such rules as the committee may make, as the minister himself. It amounts to this, as my hon. friend from Grey has said, that the minister took upon himself to refuse to the committee what no rule prevented the committee from having. Upon what principle would the hon. gentleman claim that, because he is a minister, or a member of the committee of this House- for that is what it amounts to-he could exclude from the cognizance of his colleagues certain documents which he may have in his possession? I do not think his position is tenable for an instant, because he could just as well apply that to any other document. Why is it confined to these particular schedules? They may touch upon private matters, but so far as we are concerned, they are public documents. What would prevent him from saying to any clerk in the department, This is a document that may compromise the reputation of somebody, and I forbid you from producing to the committee any document having reference to public accounts. Yet the hon. gentleman, under his interpretation of his right, could do that.

The hon. gentleman entirely forgets the difference between such a document as he refers to and these census schedules. These schedules were taken under instructions which declared to the people who gave the information that it would be held inviolate and secret; it was a contract between the people who gave the information and the department which got the information.
How long is that to be kept secret ?
Indefinitely.
Under what law ?
Under the Census Act.
It does not say so.

But the Census Act gives the minister power to make regulations for taking the census, and the instructions of the department did say so, and have said so ever since we have had a census in Canada. I have made no change in this matter, I have followed out the regulations made from time immemorial, and they are necessary for the taking of a census. If you did not make that rule you could not get the people to give the information. As it is, in some instances the people have refused and it is only by reason of the agreement that we would keep the information secret that we are able to go to the courts of law and compel people to give the information.

The order of reference instructs the committee to bring before

them all persons and papers, and that order Is above the authority of the minister or bis employees. I want to point out this fact, that in the long inquiry in 1891, when Mr. Connolly came before the committee of inquiry with their books locked up; he said they were instructed by their solicitor that these were their private papers and they had a right to refuse to expose them. What was the order of the House? It was that the books should be laid on the Table, and the books were produced and were examined. The same thing could be done in this case. I never knew an instance before the Public Accounts Committee where individuals or corporations who appeared with their private books or accounts obtained exemption from laying them before the committee. No minister has authority to say, either to an individual or an employee of the government, You need not produce these documents to committee. The authority of parliament is above the minister and should control him. I understood him at first to say that such a discussion took place regarding the secrecy of the census schedules in the committtee, and that the question was afterwards brought to this House and debated.
I did not say it was before the committee, I said the discussion took place in this House. I do not remember the details.

I asked if the minister would be good enough to point to a precedent, because I have no knowledge of any. I still think that when the House of Commons makes an order of reference to that committee it invests that committee with authority to command any official under the government to produce books or papers that may be in his custody, and the committee has a right to examine them. If a minister was invested with any such authority, it would be the easiest thing in the world for him to cover up any scaly transaction that might take place in his department by saying, This is private, and I will not allow my employees to bring it down.

The hon. gentleman knows that there is a procedure by which he can bring the matter up in due course before the House ; and if he can secure an order of the House to override my decision, he is at liberty to do so. But I must tell him frankly that he will have to get such an order before I can recede from my position.

I wish to recall to the memory of the minister that the discussion in the Public Accounts Committee went a great deal further than the point that has been raised this evening. The hon. gentleman contended there that the committee had no right to enter into the question of these schedules or to inspect them, because the

commissioner had taken an oath which prescribed secrecy and which he could not break. It was contended on the other hand that the statute gave no authority to the minister or to the Governor in Council to prescribe any such oath. I do not think tihe hon. gentleman can point to one word in the statute that authorizes any such oath to be imposed upon any official. But that is not the point I proposed to deal with. I proposed to point out a matter far more serious. The hon. gentleman, with a great deal of reference to the history of the past, said that previous governments had followed the rule he was following now. Well, assuming that previous governments had followed that rule, I would feel inclined to continue the rule, inasmuch as the public has probably been led to believe that they were giving the information under a pledge of secrecy. But it turned out that although the bon. minister was so particular about secrecy as to the census of 1901, he was not so scrupulous about the information obtained in 1891 by his predecessor. Although the officer in 1891 was sworn to secrecy, the hon. gentleman himself had no scruple whatever in obtaining from Mr. Blue the information that had been then obtained' under a similar oath of secrecy. When does the obligation of secrecy end>
? If the hon. gentleman who has been conducting this census is sworn to secrecy and if the public have been imposed upon, because they would be imposed upon in believing that the information they gave to him was absolutely secret, what may be said, if, in a year or two, all that information is to be brought into the House of Commons, published in ' Hansard,' published in the press of the country and spread broadcast over this Dominion ? Where is the good faith that the hon. minister speaks of ? In 1891 the same oath was prescribed. The information that was then given to the officers of the commissioner of that time was absolutely as secret as this information Which the hon. minister says is secret. By what right did the hon. gentleman get information upon the schedules of 1891 from certain parts of the country and then come to this House and make a statement criticising the returns of 1891 as against the returns of 1901 ? The hon. gentleman surely must be consistent. He uses the precedent of 1891 to justify his oath of secrecy. Surely the information that was then obtained should also be treated as absolutely secret and the documents that were found in the government records were just as much beyond his control as the documents obtained in 1891 are now beyond the control of the Public Accounts Committee according to his own contention. The hon. gentleman had no right to use these. The officer occupying the position that Mr. Blue occupies to-day took the oath of secrecy at that time. The information he had obtained was secret and supposed to be inviolate. By

what right was any information relating to the census of 1891 used by the present minister ? By what right did he obtain information as to schedules of 1891 which a member of the House of Commons cannot obtain in regard to the census of 1901 ? Will the hon. minister answer ?

My hon. friend (Mr. Barker) has asked a question which I think it is quite easy to answer. The census commissioners and the officers of the department in regard to the census are under oath in regard to census matters. The census commissioners of this census, I believe, have the right to investigate the census schedules of a former census.
Will the hon. gentleman tell me how and where he gets that authority ? Those who -made the farmer census were sworn to secrecy.
As officers of the department-

If the hon. gentleman will permit me, the present commissioner is not given any authority in regard to the
preceding commission. He is sworn in regard to all matters coming within hi-s knowledge in taking the census. If he gave any information in regard to the census of 1891, it would be a violation of his oath.

If the hon. gentleman will look at the Act he will find in section 20 the following
Whenever the Minister of Agriculture deems it convenient, he may, by special letter of instruction, direct any officer, census commissioner or other person employed in the execution of this Act, to make inquiry und-er oath, as to any matter connected with the taking of the census, or the ascertaining or correction of any supposed defect or inaccuracy therein ; and such officer, census commissioner or other person shall then have the same power as is vested in any court of justice, of summoning an.y person, of enforcing his attendance, and of requiring and compelling him to give evidence on oath. whether orally or in writing, and to produce such documents and things as such officer, census commissioner or other person deems requisite to the full investigation of such matter or matters.

Certainly, there is no doubt about that.
The MINISTER - OF AGRICULTURE. The statements that were laid on the Table of the House last session were the result of an investigation in regard to checking and proving the accuracy of the census of 1891. For the purpose of such proof and such checking we had to go to the census of 1891 in order to prove the correctness of the census of 1901. I have explained that on a former occasion, but, for the hon. gentleman's benefit, I can explain again that there were evident certain extraordinary discrepancies, or a startling condition
of affairs shown by a comparison of the results of the taking of the census of 1891 and the taking of the census in 1901. These results are such that there must have been some inaccuracy in one or other of the censuses, or that a very extraordinary condition of affairs had arisen in this country in regard to its progress and development between the two censuses. The first duty of the census commissioner and the officers under his charge was to see whether his own census was correct. That was investigated as far as it could be and there seemed to he no reasonable doubt that the figures and compilation were correct. Then, as an explanation of this condition of affairs, were we to accept it as a fact that Canada had absolutely retrograded during the decade, or were we to try and see whether there was another explanation of the extraordinary comparison between the two censuses. We investigated the census of 1891, I confess, largely in consequence of some allegations In regard to the taking of the census of 1891 which had been common talk throughout the country for many years- the statement that the census was padded, the statement that the census was inaccurate and the statement that the compilation was defective. We were led, perhaps, to a certain extent, by the prevalency of these statements to make this investigation.
By whom were these statements made ?
They were made by all sorts of people and they were made publicly on the floor of parliament.
Hear, hear.
They were made elsewhere through the length and breadth of Canada.
If they were made on the floor of parliament they were not secret. The commissioner was bound to keep that information secret.

The hon. gentleman is talking about another matter. The question I am speaking of was in regard to the public statements of the census of 1891 being inaccurate. These statements were very prevalent in Canada for many years after the taking of the census. I confess I was somewhat guided in my desire to look into the census of 1891 by the prevalency of these statements. I believed that the solution of the extraordinary condition of affairs might be found there. After first of all satisfying myself that the difficulty did not arise from any inaccuracy in the census of 1901. I then caused an investigation to he made. I did not give publicity to any of the facts in the schedules of 1891 which came under the category of those facts which I have stated ought to be held secret. I want my hon. friend (Mr. Barker) to understand that fully.
Did not tlie hon. gentleman refer to the names and particulars in various villages ?
The names only.
The hon. gentleman discovered that there was a family of seventeen in the province of Quebec, and he was astounded at it ?
No, I would not be astounded at that in the province of Quebec. It is quite common there.
The hon. gentleman thought it most uncommon.
I said a minute ago that I gave nothing to the public except the names. I believe I did give the names of a whole family of seventeen, but it was still only a string of names.

Did he not name a certain number of industrial establishments and say that actually upon inquiry they found old ladies knittings reported as industrial estimates ?

I think my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) is a little mistaken. I think he is confusing a former debate which he listened to many years ago with what I said on this occasion. What my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) has accused me of is of having laid on the Table of this House this information which he now accuses me of withholding. He says ^ that I am now refusing to give information which for my own purpose I gave last year. I say that I am refusing to give information now which has been given to the enumerators on a pledge of secrecy, but the information which I gave last year was merely a string of names which could in no way be considered as confidential. Last year I gave no details of property and no details of private concerns in any shape or way. In the debate which I referred to as a precedent, that question came up and gentlemen on both sides of the House took the position that the secrecy was not violated by giving the names, and that it was only as to details of business and of private property that the secrecy would be violated. It is true that last year, in consequence of the extraordinary condition of affairs which was revealed, I did make an investigation into certain facts in regard to the taking of the population in 1891, but that was all that was given to the public. I should say that the list of names was compiled from the

census of 1891 by the census officers under oath, and under that section of the law which enables them to make such an investigation as they may see fit in order to secure an accurate census. I am now asked to place the schedule before the committee, and I contend that that is contrary to the precedent which I have quoted ; contrary to the spirit and letter of the Census Act, and contrary to what is necessary for the taking of an accurate census.

The minister should have been more candid in the statement of his position. We understood from him that he had a precedent to guide him, and which to be a precedent at all must be practically identical with 'the case under discussion. The minister has shown that he has no such precedent. He cannot tell whether the circumstances in the past case are identical with the circumstances in the present case, and he does not know even whether the previous case was discussed in the House or whether a vote was taken upon it. He has to admit that he does not know whether the case which he said was a precedent ever came before the Public Accounts' Committee. The hon. gentleman told us in a very jaunty fashion that he dictated the action that was taken, and if he thinks that he can treat us in that jaunty manner I suppose he must be the judge of that himself, but we will have something to say also in regard to it. The Minister of Agriculture leads this committee to understand that he did not interfere with the public accounts committee, but that he instructed his own officials, and he announces that he has control over his own officials. Upon the minister's own confession extracted from him by the hon. member for Hamilton, the fact appears now that the minister did interfere with the investigation of the Public Accounts' Committee, and that he led the chairman to understand that a precedent existed, when as a matter of fact there is no such precedent at all. I say that the Minister of Agriculture by the presence he exercises over witnesses, and by his influence and blandishments on the chairman of the committee. wlho is susceptible to such influences, did interfere with the investigation by the committee. However willing we might be to bow for the time being to the decision which was come to in the Public Accounts' committee upon a former occasion, and which had been appealed from to the House, and had been sustained by the House In former years : we are not prepared on the mere ipse dixit of the Minister of Agriculture to accept the position which he takes to-night. The minister says that at the time he referred to in 1891 he was not in the House of Commons., He did not hear the debate ; he did not read the debate, but he asks us to accept as evidence something which he says somebody told him.

That is hardly a sufficient reason why we should pass this item. The hon. minister invokes the statute ; he says that under the statute he has a right to make regulations ; but what regulations ? The regulations for the taking of the census ? Will the hon. minister or any of the legal luminaries who support him find anywhere in the statutes one sentence that will bear the construction that for all time to come he is to control the information which we gather through the country by means of the census enumerators ? Why, the proposition is too absurd to be entertained by sensible men, much less by a committee of the House of Commons of Canada. We must approach this matter in some sense of common sense; and when the hon. minister suggests that because he has the power to pass regulations, he is therefore, for all time to come to control the free representatives of the people, and say : ' Thus far shalt thou go, and no further,' I deny the proposition absolutely. The authority with which I understand the minister to be clothed is this, that he can make regulations for the proper conduct of the officials under his control during the census enumeration. Unless he finds within the four corners of the statute a provision which says he is to be the sole confident of the secrets of this country as regards the census, I submit that it is not common sense to say that the Minister of Agriculture is to be the sole repository of the information obtained by the enumerators at the expense and for the information of the people of this country. The hon. gentleman must remember that there is a distinction between making full disclosures and making a disclosure to a committee of the House of Commons. I do not think the hon. gentleman fully appreciates that point. The hon. gentleman seems to think that so long as you are a private member of the House, so long perhaps as you are any minister of the Crown except the Minister of Agriculture, it might not be safe to trust you with a state secret; but as soon as you become Minister of Agriculture, the position changes. I claim that the right to obtain information at all is to be limited to such information as is necessarily required for the uses of the people of this country. You have no right to be inquisitorial beyond that limit. What is necessary in order to put the people of this country in a position to know and judge of their resources, their strength, and the future of this country, is what we have a right to inquire into ; and unless you can make the information available for those uses or similar uses, you have no right to obtain it at all. The House of Commons, in delegating its powers to the Public Accounts Committee, authorizes that committee to be its agent just as effectually and just as cleariy as it delegates to the Minister of Agriculture the duty of presiding over the agricultural affairs of this
country. We have just as much right, when we go into that committee, to get down to the rock foundation of things, and to find out what has been done in connection with the census, as the Minister of Agriculture lias to ascertain what his officials have been doing. Nay, more, I venture to say that if there is a distinction to be drawn, it is in favour of the Committee of the House of Commons, because we are the inquisitorial body in this case, specially charged with the duty of investigating these matters, and finding out, unless baulked completely by the hon. minister. That is what the hon. minister does not seem to like. This being a committee of investigation, presided over by a chairman, with the officials of the Census Department called to give evidence, it differs in no essential particular from an investigation before a court. These are our witnesses; we have a right to call them, I am not sure but that we have a right to call the Minister of Agriculture. I do not know but that it would be a good idea for us to do so. Perhaps he might claim privilege, and say that it might incriminate him to answer. But at all events, we have a right to call the officials for the purpose of ascertaining whether that which appears in the census is as it ought to be, and whether the work of the Census Department lias been honestly and fairly carried out. My hon. friend is not a lawyer, and I - am afraid he has not a judicial mind.
Is my hon. friend a lawyer ?
I am a farmer, I am happy to say.
A lawyer too ?

I am a farmer and an honest lawyer, or a lawyer and an honest farmer, which ever my hon. friend likes. I say that my hon. friend has not a judicial mind, with a disposition to look at both sides of a question evenly. He has one faculty of a lawyer, that of evading a question pretty effectually at certain points-a faculty which many hon. gentlemen on that side of the House possess in an eminent degree. With the experience which my hon. friend has, at all events, he will recognize that it is one of the gravest offences known to the law for any person to tamper with a witness, to approach that witness and instruct him not to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth, or to say to him, ' Couldn't you forget ? ' Well, I think it is my duty to tell the hon. minister in a most respectful way that I think intelligent men throughout the country, aside from lawyers and judges, and those specially trained in matters of this kind, will regard the Minister of Agriculture as having committed a very grave offence against the interests of this country when, without, as I understand it, consulting

the other members of the government or any authority whatever, but merely of his own motion he undertook without any authority to order his officers not to obey the instruction of the committee.
