According to Bourinot, each of the select standing committees ' shall generally be empowered to examine into all such matters and claims as may be referred to by the House, and to report from time to time their observations and opinions thereon, with power to send for persons, papers and records.' Consequently the committee had the right to bring before it any witnesses it desired and such documents as it deemed necessary. Bourinot goes on to say :
Many witnesses are examined in the course of every session before committees of the Senate and the House of Commons. It has already been stated, in the first part of this chapter, that it is usual in both houses to give committees special authority to send for witnesses or documentary evidence. Witnesses are summoned in the Commons by an order signed by. the chairman and they are bound to bring all the papers which the committee may require ; but the committee can not order the production of documents or the summoning of witnesses unless it has the necessary authority from the House to send for persons, papers and records.
In this instance the House gave the Committee on Public Accounts the authority to send for persons, papers and records. What happens should the witness refuse to obey the order of the committee ? According to Bourinot:
His conduct will be reported to the House and an order will he immediately made for his attendance at the bar or before the committee. Similar proceedings are taken when a witness refuses to answer questions.
We find a case in point cited in this work :
In the session of 1891 the committee of privileges and elections, to whom was referred a very important inquiry, reported that one of the witnesses refused to place under the immediate control of the committee certain documents which he had produced. His conduct was reported t* the House, and he was ordered to appear at the bar. He appeared and was ordered to deliver all accounts and papers to the Clerk of the House. He complied at once with the order, and the committee had consequently full control of the documents in question.

I cite this 'to show that the minister had no right to order his employees to refuse to give information to the committee or to produce the documents which the committee required. Had the refusal been reported to the House, the House could have insisted on tlie witness bringing down those papers and handing them to the committee, or have compelled them to come before the Bar of the House and hand them to the House.

My hon. friend was not in the committee when the occurrence took place. If he had been, he would have known that the chairman of the committee endorsed the course I had taken. The chairman ruled that Mr. Blue need not bring down those papers.
On whose Instructions ? The instructions of the minister, who had no authority ?
The minister did not instruct the chairman of the committee.
The minister said that he instructed his officers.
I instructed Mr. Blue, 'but not the chairman of the committee.
The hon. minister instructed the witness.

Yes, be instructed him not to bring the documents.
Mi-. SPROULE. Which he had no right to do.

The minister has a right to instruct his officer to do anything. But the chairman of the committee rules that Mr. Blue need not bring the documents. The action was the action of the committee. The hon. gentleman is1 harking up the wrong tree.
Will the hon. minister say that that was reported to the House which is a higher authority-
If the hon. _ gentleman will allow me to finish. I believe he was not present at the meeting of the committee-
I was not.

I will tell him what occurred. Mr. Blue had been ordered to appear before the committee and bring certain documents. He appeared but informed the committee that he had not the documents. The committee discussed whether he should be required to bring the documents. Certain members, including the hon. member from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) contended that he should bring the documents. The Minister of Agriculture, who is not a member of the committee, asked leave to explain. He stated that he had

ordered Mr. Blue not to bring the documents and gave the grounds for his position, which I need not repeat. In the meantime, as I said a few minutes ago. the hon. gentleman is barking up the wrong tree. He says the Minister of Agriculture dictated to the committee and gave instructions to his officer contrary to the order of the committee

	'
Contrary to the order of the House.
No.
Yes.

Well, if the hon. gentleman thinks so. But I have explained the case so thoroughly that I need not go further than to quote from Bourinot, the authority on which the hon. gentleman relies, page 337:
Whilst members have every facility afforded them to obtain all the information they require on matters of public concern, occasions may arise when the government will feel constrained to refuse certain papers on the ground that their production would be inconvenient or contrary to the public interest.

I have given the authority that the House delegates to the committee and shown the right of the committee to demand that persons and papers ho brought. I have given the rule that compels the witness to bring with him such documents as are required. I followed this up by showing what was (Jone when the witness refused, no matter who instructed him. The case was reported to the House, which ordered the witness to be brought to the Bar, and then directed him to de-ooo
liver the papers to the House, and the House returned them to the committee. I showed that the House has higher authority than the witness or the minister
Nobody denies that.

I cau only say that if I had been there, I should have tried to bring it before the House, and I have taken the first opportunity afforded me to try to review the matter, for when I saw the course taken by the minister, reported in the newspapers, I thought it a high-handed proceeding, quite beyond his authority as a minister and justified by no rule or precedent.

I do not wish to occupy the time of the House, but I desire to call attention to the instructions the Minister of Agriculture gave to his officers on the subject of the secrecy to be observed with regard to names. He now seems to draw some distinction between names and other particulars in the schedules, and claims he had the right to do what he did in sending lists of names of the census of 1891 to different parts of the country, to <persons in no way connected with the census, to obtain information from them, and then use the information gained from them, and the names, in this House for political purposes. I propose to read from his own instructions to show that the names are as much secret as any other part of the information he had obtained and that he has no more right to deal with the names than to deal with the particulars of property given in the schedules. I might remind the hon. gentleman that he sent a special circular all over the province of Quebec emphasizing these instructions and particularly informing the people that everything connected with the census was absolutely secret. We on this side of the House do not admit that the government had any right to Impose the oath of secrecy. The statute certainly does not authorize it. It authorizes the government to settle forms of oaths to be taken by the officers for the purposes of the census, but in no way does it authorize that an officer shall be prevented from giving information as to what the schedules contain when called upon by the committee of the House. This is one clause of the instructions
Many persons imagine that the census schedules may be in some wav used as a sort of advertisement for them or as a reflection upon them. But the fact is that these schedules are never seen except by the commissioners-
If that is so, how does the hon. gentleman get the information upon which he



made a long speech in this House last session ?
-these schedules are never seen except by the commissioner and others engaged in taking and compelling the census, who, besides being sworn officers bound not to divulge any individual information, care very little for, and have no Interest in, the several statements contained in them. The names

So, here the names are particularly mentioned as something secret.
-are taken in the census schedules simply for a check upon the returns, and to afford opportunity to correct any palpable error."
What is the hon. gentleman (Mr. Barker) reading ?

From chap. 1 of the instructions, page 7, the 4th paragraph.
In other words the enumeration of names is a necessary guarantee of good faith and correctness and it has no other object.
Now, will the hon. gentleman tell me that there is anything connected with the census that is not secret, if any part be ? Does not that convey the impression that these men get the information for the commissioners and that the names are held secret, as well as everything else ? The hon. gentleman has issued these instructions to his officials, but he sent a circular throughout the province of Quebec repeating them and informing the people how secret these would be. Here is a paragraph in the instructions, showing that the names are used for a particular purpose, and yet it turns out that the census of 1891 has been used by the hon. gentleman for political purposes, and he made a speech here upon information obtained outside the census officials of 1891, though they were also sworn to secrecy.

The hon. gentleman has spoken about the names as being just as secret as other parts of the census. Let me quote from a debate which occurred in regard to the census of 1S91 on this very question. The debate arose in 1893, and in the course of some remarks an hon. member of the House, after quoting the instructions in the census of that date, says :
It will be found that the letter of instructions scarcely goes so far as to prevent the names of persons from being given. There was this view to be considered. Although no wri:-ten instructions were given, the census enumerators and commissioners have found that people are sensitive in giving information which might in any manner become known to competitors in their busines.	[DOT]
Further on he says : ,
It would appear therefor that there is nothing in the instructions, either verbal or written, which would preclude the giving of the nam=s of persons who own and carry on industrial establishments, and I can see no reason-and I think it would be difficult to find a valid reason-why the names of persons who carry on Mr. BARKER.
these establishments should be withheld. When we go further than that to details of the business which a person carries on under his own name. I think we approach ground where there is very good reason why it should be withheld. Great difficulty has been experienced in the case of persons carrying on a single industry, I mean one which in the tabulations is not united with any others carrying on a similar industry. ... In these cases it was found that several were very loath to give the details asked for because they were by themselves and the figures would give information as to the details of their single business.

I understand that the hon. gentleman, having looked into the matter is willing to give the names and descriptions.
The reply was :
Yes. I see no objection.
Now, these words which I have quoted were uttered by the then acting Minister of Agriculture in the Conservative government, the Hon. George E. Foster. He took exactly the ground_I am taking here to-night. That ground was based upon precedent, and the ground I talje now is based upon precedent in the census of 1891. Reference was made in that debate to the censuses of 1S71 and 1881, and the same course was taken by tile then existing governments in regard to the question of divulging the details of the census schedules. I have continued exactly the course and policy which were followed by the governments having in charge the preceding censuses.

Before the item is adopted, I wish to ask the minister one or two questions. It is said that the expense of taking the census of 1901 far exceeded the cost of taking the census of 1891, and consequently it is proper for us to inquire why that cost is so much greater. The items that I may mention perhaps are small, but yet many small items put together make a very large one. I find, for example, in the case of Beauharnois, in the province of Quebec, on page D-219 of the Auditor General's Report, the commissioner was allowed $30.75 for meals for enumerators while receiving instructions. This does not seem to have been a general practice, and I have been wondering why this commissioner should be so favoured. However, he was not so much favoured as another commissioner, the one for Chambly and VerchiSres. On page D-222 I find that this commissioner was allowed the sum of $132 for meals for enumerators during instructions. Now, why should this commissioner be allowed to give his enumerators a champagne luncheon when they met together for the purpose of receiving instructions, while the poor enumerators in the province of Ontario had to pay for their own dinner ? It seems to me that is unfair. But that is not the chief point. It shows to me that these accounts have been passed without any care whatever, that no special care has been taken by the department in examining into the correctness of

these accounts, but that every item sent in by the commissioners was allowed by the department.
The MINISTER OB'' AGRICULTURE. An allowance of that kind was made to the enumerators when they went to receive their instructions ; they were allowed their expenses. This particular case, as the hon. gentleman says, is a curious one. I am informed that the commissioner paid for the meals of the enumerators, and they were not allowed anything individually for that purpose. The account appears here as paid to the commissioner. I find that enumerators seem to have been allowed expenses of various sums running from $2 up to .$4 and over, notwithstanding the fact that the commissioner had to provide for their accommodation. They also received their ordinary day's pay of $3, as each enumerator seems to have been allowed $9.

In the county of Hal-ton I notice that meals were not allowed to the enumerators, and that no allowance whatever was given to the commissioner for meals for them.
Because the enumerators paid for their own meals.

Certainly, and I think they should have done so in Chambly and Vercheres also. However, that is not a big matter, but it was one of the matters that go to swell the increase. There is another matter I desire to draw the hon. minister's attention to. That is the taking of the census in Burrard. My attention was drawn to this through reading an open letter written by Mr. Wm. McCraney, formerly member of this House for the county of Halton, now residing in British Columbia, a gentleman whom I knew very well during his long residence in that county, a gentleman who occupied a seat in this House, I think, for two parliaments, a gentleman whose word would be accepted by any one who had the pleasure of knowing him. I believe' he would be incapable of prevaricating or making a misstatement 2224
in regard to this matter. Mr. McCraney draws particular attention to the cost of taking the census in Burrard, and this is one of the places where it seems to me the cost has been swelled enormously. McGregor-

I have not tire details to show whether the retaking of that part of the country cost so much as that, hut I am only stating what I know at the present time off-hand in regard to the taking of the census in that particular part of the country.

I was quite aware of the fact, and I have no doubt Mr. McCraney was also aware of the fact of the ' Islander ' having been lost, of the documents relating to the census having also been lost, and that the census had to be retaken, but the hon. minister is mistaken when he presumes that this accounts for the extraordinary difference between the careful estimate of Mr. McCraney and tire actual cost of taking the census. Dividing that into1 two equal parts, it would show that the cost of retaking the census, or the additional cost on account of the loss of the * Islander ' would be $2,220. If you deduct $2,220 from the total cost of $17,G28, you would still have a cost, of $15,407 for taking the census, which Mr. McCraney says ought to have been taken for $10,000. I do not think for one moment that the loss of the ' Islander ' explains the matter. Besides the minister is mistaken when he says that the commissioner had to go through this district. I do not think that the commissioner ever went into that district at all. The men who were paid were Geo. Pollard, Robert Patrick and Henry E. Brown, for taking the census in that district where the records were lost, so that the extended time of 210 days for which the commissioner was employed was certainly not on account of his having to go up there a second time, because he does not appear to have been there even once. I am afraid that there is more truth than poetry in the statement of Mr. McCraney when he calls Vancouver the most corrupt constituency he 'can find in the Dominion.

When Mr. Kelly went home he wrote a letter, dated Marmora, 24tli of March, but before I read the letter, permit me to say, we complain that toe minister did not send' out any fixed schedule of remuneration, and that it resulted in the commissioners' coming down here and interviewing the minister, and no doubt if they gave a good account of their stewardship the minister paid the amount they claimed. When I met you In the House of Commons on Thursday last in company with Mr. Lott.

The Ontario elections are coming off the end of May or the beginning of June. Mr. B. O. Lott is the unanimous choice of the Liberal convention. Yiour old servant,

You siay the Minister of Agriculture has fully considered my account and that an additional amount of $300 has been allowed me. I will accept the $300.

I certainly feel I am entitled to the full amount of my account anid I urge you to look more carefully Into the matter as it will injure our cause here.

Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) I am asking the Chairman that question.

speechtext: It is the census ; it is a very wide question.
If toe hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Ross) would stop writing and listen to what is going on he would understand.
There is not so much Interest In it as to cause any one to listen.

I can inform the superannuated gentleman that I am within my rights before this committee. I am reading a letter addressed to the minister in respect to the payment of a census account, and that is about as close up to the mark as we generally get in this House. I am pointing out that this Mr. Kelly came down here with the Reform nominee whom he promised to support, and he is paid by the country to the tune of $053.14. I complain that the minister has left himself open by the Instructions he issued to this kind of thing. If the commissioner gives a good account of his stewardship, the hon. minister instructs the department to pay the account, and it is paid.	.

I cannot remember the letter in question. I may have seen it or I may not have seen it; but I can assure toe hon. gentleman that Mr. Kelly's account was carefully scrutinized, and when he was paid the extra amount, it was on the explanations furnished by him when he came down and interviewed me. Mr. Kelly's statement was supported by Mr. Lott, as appears on the face of that letter,
It is a copy of a letter from the hon. gentleman's own department.
I take it that the hon. gentleman is reading a copy of a letter which is authentic. I do not remember the letter, and I cannot say anything about it.
Do you remember the interview ?

I remember the interview with Mr. Kelly; I do not remember seeing Mr. Lott. But it is quite a common thing for people who want to get their accounts straightened out to bring friends with them. In that case my heart seems to be softened. I have no doubt Mr. Kelly gave satisfactory explanations to show why he should be paid that amount of money. I am sure I would not have paid it for any political reasons.
When does the minister expect to complete the taking of the census-I mean collecting the information V

The enumeration is practically completed. There are a few items scattered about which we have to write about. But practically the whole enumeration is completed, and the accounts in connection with it are all closed. There are a few complaints still in existence, some of which may on investigation be conceded, but I think they will be very few.
Within the past month information was being collected in my county, and I wondered if that was a very general thing.

I may say that when anything appears on a schedule inconsistent with some other statement in it. it is the duty of the officers here to communicate with the enumerator who made the schedule and obtain explanations. That is part of the work of compilation and checking. Occasionally letters are sent to enumerators who took information which on the surface is not quite explainable. and when it is explained, the information is complete.

The minister promised that he would explain the item on page D-184 concerning an assistant commissioner in North Ontario. This is the gentleman who some time ago was concerned with a little ballot stuffing there in the interest of the Liberal party. He is paid for fifty-eight days at $3.50 a day. I would like to know what that is for.
Mr. Roach was appointed to assist Mr. Graham in consequence of the great length of the constituency.

Have all the accounts in connection with the county of Lisgar, Mani-Hon. Mr. FISHER.
toba, been paid, or are there any disputed accounts there ?
All the Manitoba accounts have been settled.
I understood the minister to make a statement a few days ago with reference to a proposition to keep a permanent staff of officers for the census. Has he decided anything in regard to that ?

I made the suggestion that it would be a wise thing to keep a very small permanent staff for census work and to prepare certain statistics between the census years. I believe it would be very advantageous to the country, but I have not been able to submit any such scheme to my colleagues, and they have not yet considered it. Consequently it is all unsettled as yet.

I am quite sure that the taking of the census for 1901 has not been satisfactory to the people of Canada. The cost of taking that census, as stated by the hon. minister, will amount to about $1,150,000 before it is completed, a good deal more than double the cost of taking the census of 1891. I find that the enumerators were instructed to take some of their figures from the assessment rolls of the province of Ontario. It is well understood that the municipal assessors do their work in the spring in every township of Ontario. I have here a copy of the assessment blanks put in the hands of every assessor of Ontario, and the number of columns is very large, thirty-four. In many of these columns are found exactly the same questions as are asked by the enumerators, and in case of death the enumerators were instructed to verify their figures from the assessment rolls.
No.
I understood that that was done in some parts of Ontario.
No.
How did they get the details ?

They got them from the people they were questioning. They asked them what death occurred in the family. In Ottawa the death returns were compared with those in the assessment rolls, but the enumerators-did not in any case take their information from these rolls.
Why were instructions given to compare them ?
Simply to see how they compared.

In the correspondence some of the enumerators have said that they took
the deaths from the municipal clerks and the assessment rolls in the different counties. I read the letters myself, so that I have personal knowledge of what I am stating. If the hon. minister feels it to he his duty to make a comparison between the reports of his enumerators and the returns by the different assessors in Ontario, and if he proposes to keep a permanent staff, I would suggest that he could reduce the cost of taking the census In Ontario very much by utilizing the assessment rolls in the different municipalities. Here are the people in these older counties, who are decreasing in population every year, in every municipality the assessor every year goes over the same farms, interviews the same families, fills in the same columns, and these are returned to the provincial government and no doubt also to the Dominion government. And! it would be worthy of the hon. gentleman's attention to see if a large reduction could not be made in the taking of the census by utilizing these assessment rolls, which are always up-to-date.
I think the suggestion a very good one, and I am glad to find that my hon. friend has such confidence in my continued tenure of the office.
There were certain disputed accounts in the county of Lisgar, when were these settled ?
A long time ago-nearly a year back.
I understood that they were settled at the time of the by-eiection ?
We discussed that last year.
Is there any Information in the published census returns which is compiled from any source except from the returns of the enumerators ?
There is not.
Waiving the question of our right to get these secrets, are we to understand that the printed document corresponds in every instance with the returns of the enumerators?

Yes.
ill-. LENNOX. Has it been brought to the knowledge of the minister that the opinion widely prevails that certain liberties have been taken with the returns made by the enumerators? For instance, that the sex of the individual has been changed?
That has never been brought to my attention.

That is, a person returned as a woman was converted to a man
and vice versa. I do not know which is the greater offence. Although I am not able to prove the fact, I have reason to believe that the opinion is fairly well founded.

There is a very large and important item with regard to "cold storage and dairying, $220,000, an increase of $10,000. What is this increase for, and in what way does the hon gentleman divide this large amount of money among the various branches of his department ?

I have not got the papers under my hand, and therefore cannot give the figures exactly with regard to the division, but in general terms I may say that that vote, which is under Professor Robertson's management, is divided in this way. We have what we call the fruit division, the poultry division, the live stock divisou. the cold storage division, the pushing of our commerce in foreign markets, and then the general office expenses here at Ottawa for that division. I would not like, off-hand, to give the figures, hut the cold storage division takes the largest amount. That covers not only cold storage work in the country, which comprises the bonus paid to the creameries and the refrigerator car service in the railways. I do not think that this year there has been a bonus of any kind on cold storage warehouses in Canada. I think these are finished, and also the cold storage and cool chambers on board the ocean steamers. I omitted a number of divisions. There is the dairy division proper, which includes the running of the creameries in the North-west Territories, the management of one or two creameries in Nova Scotia, the management of the cool curing rooms for cheese which were established last year, and the general instruction work with regard to dairying. The live stock division, under Mr. Hodson, includes work in connection with the live stock associations in the different provinces, work in connection with the fairs and exhibitions, assistance to the institute work in the various provinces, and also work in relation to the great agricultural gatherings of the year, such as the Guelph' Fat Stock Show, the fat stock show at Amherst, and the various sales of live stock which have been organized and carried on more or less under the control, though not under the actual administration, of the live stock commissioner. The fruit division includes the administration of the Fruit Marks Act, including a certain amount of supervision of, and investigation into, the growth of fruit in the country ; the management of packing, and suggestion and instruction in regard to it, and "also some slight investigation into the condition in which our fruits arrive in foreign markets and how they are handled there, as well as the gathering of informa-

tion which will aid our shippers in packing and the management of shipments. The poultry division deals chiefly with the business of eggs and poultry meat in the country, trying to show that our people here can successfully and properly fatten poultry for the home and foreign markets ; and we have also been gathering more or less information with regard to poultry management for the production of both eggs and meat. The headquarters staff includes Professor Robertson's own salary and travelling expenses, the main officers here at Ottawa and the accountant work for the whole of these different branches. The increase of $ 10,000 is due to a general expansion of the work almost entirely. About $3,000 or $4,000 is additional for the live stock division, [DOT]and another portion is additional for the foreign markets division. Speaking offhand and from memory, I think we are not proposing to spend more during the coming year on the cold storage division or on the dairy division than we did last year. The fruit inspection, I think, is costing a little more, chiefly in travelling expenses, due to the fact that the fruit inspectors are asked for the year round, while we originally intended to have them only during six or seven months of the year." I do not recall any other increases that are at all considerable. But, of course, in this, as in all other branches, there is a constant slight tendency to increase salaries. And I may say, in explanation, that there is a constant effort on the part of people to tempt away the men who are engaged in this work who have expert knowledge. I am constantly being brought face to face with the fact that in the United States the colleges and experimental stations and large business concerns want to get our men, offering them high salaries and advantageous positions. And it is only by raising the salaries to a certain extent that I am able to keep the men. But I want to do credit to our officers by saying

and I say it with the greatest pride and satisfaction-that the officers of the Department of Agriculture are interested in their work, are patriotic in their work, and are willing and glad to stay here at prices much below what they could get were they to desert Canada and go to foreign lands. By reason of their interest in their work and their patriotic feeling in the development of the country, the best of them have refused advantageous offers rather than leave the service of Canada.

The minister has gone over the subjects treated of in the different divisions. But I am bound to say that the answer as to the amount of money to be spent on any division is not very clear. We do not know, for instance, what is to be spent for the extension of markets or what amount for cold storage.
I am sorry I can not give that this evening.

But I shall be glad to give the hon. gentleman an opportunity later on to get all the information he wants. I have the information prepared by officers of the department but the papers are not here. If the hon. gentleman would like, I would suggest, if the discussion of the census is closed, that we might call the census item carried but the House will have every opportunity discuss the vote my hon. friend from Wentworth (Mr. Smith) lias referred to. And i would call that vote to give Him every opportunity to learn whatever details he may wish to know.
I understand that the hon. minister will, call this vote for the cold storage division again V
Yes.

I am sure that the hon. minister knows the inconvenience of an arrangement of that kind. This is a very imp irtant service, and the committee will certainly require to have the information in considerable detail. The minister has told us in general terms something about the service. But as my hon. friend from Wentworth (Mr. Smith) says, no details are given. I should suggest that, so far as the census matter is concerned, that item may be considered as dealt with for the present at least. But this other matter should stand until the hon. minister is prepared to give us the information. I mean by that that this item relating to cold storage does not pass at all to-night.
That is what I proposed. Let the census item be declared carried, if my hon. friends opposite say the discussion-

My attention has just been called to the fact that all the items have been passed with the exception of the census. Therefore, I am afraid we shall have to hold that as a hostage a little longer until the hon. gentleman is prepared to give the information we are asking for.

I was suggesting to pass the census item-let the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) not shake his head until he has heard me-and I will ask the Chairman to call the item of $220,000 for the express purpose of affording a full discussion on that item. And I pledge myself to have here the information asked for. If that is agreeable, I will propose it; if not I am in the hands of the hon. gentlemen. When that item passed some weeks ago I gave a pledge that an opportunity wrould be given to discuss it, and I do not wish to depart from that pledge.
When will the matter be taken up again ?

I would not like to take it up this week,

because the chief officer of that division is away. I may take it up some day next Week, when I will have all my papers with me.
Dominion arsenal, $150,000.

This item is for the* Dominion arsenal at Quebec, where cartridges and ammunition for artillery are manufactured in, a government factory. This money will be used in the payment of wages and the purchase of material chiefly. The amount of wages is estimated at about $72,000, and the materials over $100,000 for the manufacture of cartridges. In the shell factory the wages amount to about $12,000, and materials to $5,000. In the artillery workshop, the wages amount to $10,000 and the materials to $8,000. I may say generally with regard to 'this factory, that it has recently been greatly improved and increased in capacity. While we were manufacturing a million rounds a few years ago. last year we manufactured about 7,000,000 rounds of ball cartridge. The capacity of the factory for the present year will be something like 12,000.000 or 13,000.000. For the present year it is expected that over and above the ordinary requirements, there will be manufactured 2,000,000 rounds, which will go towards making a reserve of ammunition.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE (Hon. Sir F. W. Borden).

speechtext: Will the minister explain about the miniature ammunition, and how it is distributed 1

Last year of that there was manufactured 415,000 rounds. As my hon. friend knows, the old exploded shells of cartridges are used for that purpose, and a very much smaller quantity of powder is used in making them. This ammunition is found to be very valuable for practice at short range, I think only twenty-live yards distance is necessary to practice with this ammunition. It is found very useful at camps and places where the ranges are not safe for the use of long range cartridges.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I understood the minister was going. to supply it to the cadet schools free. I am informed they cannot get any.

Because we have not yet been able to make a sufficient quantity. Small quantities have been supplied to the cadets Within the last month or two. I hope next year we will be able to supply it free in large quantities.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: Are there any items coming up in the supplementary estimates on which we can discuss the militia question '1

Yes, there will be in the supplementary estimates an item upon which
the whole condition of the militia and the question of defence can be discussed, and upon which I expect to make a statement to the House with reference to those matters.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: I may point out to the minister that our friends across the way have set us an example.that it might be well for us to consider. I do not find any fault with the Dominion arsenal being stationed at Quebec, except that from a strategic view point, in case of invasion of this country, Quebec would certainly be one of the first places invested. If our enemy could possibly control the approach to the river, he might possibly control the approach by land also. Our American cousins have their main arsenal at Springfield, quite a distance from the seaboard, and they also have another one at Rock island, on the Mississippi river. I had the privilege of going through both of them, and they make no secret of stating that the object of having them so far inland and away from the seacoast is to make them practically absolutely safe in time of war from attack. I would suggest to the minister that in case he proposes to erect a larger arsenal, it might be well to consider the advisability of placing it further inland.

I quite agree with my hon. friend, and there is a great deal of force in what he says. However, we know that it is an easy matter to move the cartridges the moment they are manufactured to points inland and store them in magazines. Two or three places are to be constructed in the present year for that purpose. I agree with him that in the near future it will be necessary to construct another cartridge factory, and when that time comes, I think some inland point should be selected. It has been in my own mind that possibly some point near the city of Ottawa might be a convenient place, where there is good railway communication inland, and where stores of this kind could be moved rapidly and safely.
